en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Recitation for Illuminating the Summary of the *Paṭṭhāna*. 1.
The Root Condition (*hetu-paccaya*)

What is the root condition (*hetupaccaya*)? Greed (*lobha*) is a root condition; hatred (*dosa*), delusion (*moha*), non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*) are root conditions.

What phenomena are the conditionally arisen (*paccayuppanna*) of the root condition? They are the mental states and mental factors co-nascent with greed, as well as the material groupings (*rūpakalāpa*) of phenomena;
likewise those co-nascent with hatred, co-nascent with delusion, co-nascent with non-greed, co-nascent with non-hatred, and co-nascent with non-delusion.

Mental states (citta) and mental concomitants (cetasika), as well as material groups (rūpakalāpa), which arise by way of the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya), are "states arisen from root-cause conditions" (hetupaccayuppanna).

Those called "conascent material groups" consist of the kamma-born material phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) that possess roots, and the consciousness-born material phenomena during the course of existence (pavatti) that possess roots.
Therein, the "moment of rebirth-linking" refers to the arising-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness. The "time of the course of existence" refers to...
It is said [to exist] from the moment of the stationing of the rebirth-linking consciousness until the time of death.

In what sense is it a "cause" (hetu), and in what sense is it a "condition" (paccaya)? It is a cause in the sense of being a root (mūla), and a condition in the sense of being an assistant (upakāraka).
Therein, the state of being a root of the root-phenomena such as greed and so forth, which are mentioned in the *Mūlayamaka*, is called the "sense of being a root. That sense of being a root—
In our *Mūlayamakadīpanī*, this has already been illustrated by the simile of the tree.
Furthermore, suppose there is a man whose mind is bound to a certain woman.
As long as he does not abandon that attachment, then with reference to that woman, that man’s bodily, verbal, and mental kamma—arising from greed and co-nascent with greed—will continue to occur.

Furthermore, the material phenomena born of consciousness continue to occur for a long time. All those mental states, mental factors, and material phenomena in that woman are rooted in lust and greed.
That greed is their cause (*hetu*) in the sense of being their root, and it is their condition (*paccaya*) in the sense of being an auxiliary support;
therefore, it is the causal condition (*hetu-paccaya*). This same method applies to the remaining objects of lust, by way of the lust arising in relation to them.
Regarding greed that has arisen; regarding hatred that has arisen by way of hating in reference to objects provocative of hatred;
and regarding delusion that has arisen by way of being deluded in reference to objects provocative of delusion.
In this context, just as the roots of a tree, having become firmly established within the earth itself, [absorb] the essence of the earth...
Taking up the sap of water, they nourish that tree up to its very top; thus, the tree stands growing for a long time.

Likewise, greed, having become firmly established through the process of attachment toward various objects, takes up the essence of the agreeable and the essence of the pleasant in those respective objects, and [extends] the associated mental states... up to...
They bring about transgressions of body and speech; that is, they cause one to incur either a transgression of body or a transgression of speech.
Likewise, hatred (dosa), by way of hating, takes hold of the flavor of what is unlovely and the flavor of what is unpleasant;
and delusion (moha), by way of being deluded, increases the flavor of aimless mental wandering among various objects—so it should be said. Thus, these three, while bringing [these things] forth...
When associated mental states (sampayutta-dhamma) rejoice and exult in objects such as those that provoke lust, they cause them to continue for a long time as if they were acting themselves;

and the associated states likewise proceed in that manner. While the associated states are proceeding in that way, even the groups of co-nascent material phenomena (sahajāta-rūpa-kalāpa) proceed in exactly the same way. In this regard, regarding the associated states...
"He brings toward" means that both the forms that are dear and the flavors that are pleasant bring [the mind] into proximity with the associated mental states; this is the meaning.
In the case of the bright side (sukkapakkha), when that man perceives the danger in sensual pleasures, he then abandons that [lustful] mind, and non-greed arises directed toward that woman.
Previously, at the time when [there was] greed rooted in that woman directed toward her—

Impure bodily, verbal, and mental actions were occurring. Now, at this time as well, pure bodily, verbal, and mental actions rooted in non-greed are occurring—whether they be the restraints of the moral discipline of one gone forth, the preliminary stages of jhāna, or the attainments of jhāna.
That non-greed is both the cause of these in the sense of being their root, and the condition for them in the sense of being a supportive factor.
Therefore, it is the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*). This same method applies to the remaining opposites of greed:
non-greed (*alobha*) as the opposite of greed, non-hatred (*adosa*) as the opposite of hatred, and non-delusion (*amoha*) as the opposite of delusion.
In this regard, non-greed—like the roots of trees—having abandoned greed for objects that provoke greed, [partakes] in the flavor of the bliss of seclusion from greed.

Having increased that happiness, as if making the mental states associated with it rejoice and exult, it causes them to increase up to the bliss of meditative attainment (*jhāna-samāpatti*) or up to the bliss of the path and its fruition (*magga-phala*).
Likewise, it should be said that non-hatred (*adosa*) increases the flavor of the bliss of seclusion from hatred regarding objects provocative of hatred,
and non-delusion (*amoha*) increases the flavor of the bliss of seclusion from delusion regarding objects provocative of delusion.
Thus, while these three factors cause the associated mental states among the wholesome states to rejoice and exult, they themselves continue to proceed for a long time as if doing so;
and the associated states likewise proceed in that manner. And while the associated states proceed in that way, even the groups of co-nascent material phenomena proceed in exactly the same way.

In this context, *lobhavivekasukharasa* means the essence of the happiness of seclusion from greed. *Viveka* is the act of separating or departing; it is the seclusion (*viveka*) of greed, hence "seclusion from greed" (*lobhaviveka*).
The happiness in that seclusion from greed is "the happiness of seclusion from greed" (*lobhavivekasukha*). What is meant is: the happiness arisen dependent upon the seclusion from greed.
That very thing is the "essence" (*rasa*), thus "the essence of the happiness of seclusion from greed"—this is the compound. This is the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* in the Abhidhamma.

Furthermore, according to the method of the "That Which Is" (*hattantanaya*), the two factors consisting of delusion—defined as ignorance—and greed—defined as craving—are the roots of all phenomena pertaining to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Hatred, moreover, is a root of evil that is a natural outflow of greed.

The two factors consisting of non-delusion—defined as true knowledge—and non-greed—defined as the element of renunciation—are the [roots] of the phenomena pertaining to the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭadhamma*).
These are the roots. Non-hatred (*adosa*), however, is a beautiful root that is the outflow (*nissanda*) of non-greed (*alobha*).

Thus, these six kinds of roots serve as conditions for mental and physical phenomena (*nāmarūpa-dhamma*), whether they arise simultaneously with them or not. This is the method found in the Suttantas.
The exposition of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) is completed.
2. Object Condition (Ārammaṇapaccaya).

What is the object condition? All states of consciousness and mental factors, all material phenomena, Nibbāna, and all conceptual descriptions (paññatti) are object conditions. Indeed, there is not a single state that does not [serve as an object].
Mind is not an object for mental factors. In brief, however, objects are sixfold:
visible-form object, sound object, odor object, taste object, tangible-object, and mental-object.
Which phenomena are the conditionally arisen results of the object-condition? All phenomena consisting of mind and mental factors are [the results] of the object-condition.
Conditionally arisen. Indeed, there is no such thing as a consciousness that arises without an object—whether that object be real or unreal.
In this context, a present visible-form object is the object-condition for two types of eye-consciousness;
a present sound object is [the object-condition] for two types of ear-consciousness; a present odor object...
The present taste-object is a condition by way of object for the two types of nose-consciousness mind.
The present tangible-object is a condition by way of object for the three types of body-consciousness mind.
Those five present objects are a condition by way of object for the three types of mind-element mind. All of them—past, future, and present—are [conditions].

All five kinds of sense objects—whether pertaining to the three periods of time or timeless—and all mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) are the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), as appropriate, for the seventy-six types of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa-citta).

In what sense is it an "object" (ārammaṇa), and in what sense is it a "condition" (paccaya)? It is an "object" in the sense of being that which is to be apprehended by consciousness and its mental factors; it is a "condition" in the sense of being a supportive factor.

And here, in the sense of "to be clung to," the act of clinging (*ālambana-kiriyā*) refers to the mental activity of the mind and its concomitants in grasping an object, that is, the act of taking up an object.

Just as in the world there is a particular kind of iron ore called "iron-lover" (*ayokantaka*)—so named in the sense that it desires or longs for the iron element—and when it comes near a lump of iron, it faces toward that lump of iron as if desiring and longing for it; so too...
It moves. Either it approaches that iron bar itself, or it draws the iron bar toward itself;
the iron bar moves toward it, or it approaches that [iron bar]. This is called the "act of seizing" (*ālambana-kiriya*) of the iron hook.
In the same way, the act of seizing by the mind and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*) upon objects (*ārammaṇa*) is to be understood. It is not only upon objects...

There is merely an object. However, when mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) arise within the continuum of a being, they arise moment by moment precisely at the instant the objects enter the range of the six sense doors; and having arisen, they cease moment by moment.
This is just as sounds from a drum arise on the surface of the drum only at the very moment it is struck here and there by the hand.
They arise moment by moment, and having arisen, they cease moment by moment.
When the sounds of a lute arise, they arise moment by moment precisely at the various points on the lute strings where they are struck by the plectrum;
and having arisen, they cease moment by moment. This is also the case during the occurrence of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) for one who is sleeping.

At the time of death in a previous existence, those kamma, kamma-nimitta, and gati-nimitta that have entered the range of the six sense doors serve as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for the life-continuum consciousnesses (bhavaṅga-citta).
The exposition of the object-condition is concluded. 3.
The Dominant Condition (adhipati-paccaya).

The predominance condition (adhipatipaccaya) is twofold: the object-predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya) and the co-nascent predominance condition (sahajātādhipatipaccaya). Among these, what is the object-predominance condition?

Of the objects mentioned under the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya), those objects which are exceedingly desired, exceedingly lovely, exceedingly agreeable, and highly esteemed—those objects constitute the object-predominance condition.
In this context, "excessively desirable" (*atīṭṭhāni*) refers to objects that, whether they are desirable by their own nature or undesirable, have been excessively craved by a particular person;
these are what are called "excessively desirable" here.

As for those [objects], in terms of phenomena (*dhamma*), they occur in two types of unwholesome mind-arising rooted in hatred, in two types of mind-arising characterized by delusion, and in body-consciousness mind-arisings accompanied by suffering.

Excluding those [three], all remaining sense-sphere consciousnesses and mental factors, all fine-material and immaterial supramundane consciousnesses and mental factors, and all very desirable material phenomena, are [objects].
Among these, for one who esteems them, objects that have sense-sphere phenomena as their object are the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*). For one who does not esteem them, they are not.

There is no predominance condition by way of object (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*). However, there are no attainers of jhāna who do not hold dear the sublime jhānas they themselves have attained, nor are there any noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) who do not hold dear the supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) they themselves have attained.
Which states are the states arisen through that condition? They are the eight consciousnesses rooted in greed and the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses.
The four sense-sphere functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge and the eight supramundane consciousnesses are the conditionally arisen states for that condition.
Among these, the six mundane objects are the conditions for the consciousness rooted in greed.

The seventeen mundane wholesome states are the conditions for the four types of wholesome consciousness dissociated from knowledge. Furthermore, those same wholesome states, as well as the lower paths and fruits and Nibbāna, [are the conditions for the supramundane].
[Nibbāna] is the object of the four wholesome states associated with knowledge; it is the object of the paths and fruits of Arahantship and of the four functional states associated with knowledge;
and it is the object of the eight supramundane consciousnesses.

In what sense is it an "object" (ārammaṇa), and in what sense is it a "predominant factor" (adhipati)? It is an object in the sense of being something to be apprehended (ālambitabba), and a predominant factor in the sense of exercising sovereignty (ādhipacca).
Predominance (*adhipati*). What is the meaning of predominance? The sense of lordship over the mind and mental factors that arise having made oneself weighty is the meaning of predominance.
In the world, the objects of the predominance-condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*) should be regarded as masters, and the phenomena produced by those conditions should be regarded as servants.
In the Sutasoma Jātaka, King Porisāda, esteeming human flesh, abandoned his kingdom for the sake of human flesh and wandered in the forest.
Therein, the qualities of smell and taste in human flesh are the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*).
King Porisāda’s mind rooted in greed is the phenomenon arisen through conditions (*paccayuppannadhamma*). King Sutasoma [practiced] the Dhamma of truth.

Having made the True Dhamma weighty, and having sacrificed his royal prosperity, his kinsmen, his assembly, and even his own life, he again fell into the hands of King Porisāda. In this case, the True Dhamma is the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya*).
King Sutasoma’s wholesome consciousness is the phenomenon arisen through conditions (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*). This same method applies to all objects that are treated as weighty.

What is the conascence-predominance condition? Four states that have attained the status of predominance are the predominance condition: desire (*chanda*), consciousness (*citta*), energy (*viriya*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).

Which states are the conditionally arisen results of that condition? The consciousness and mental factors associated with the predominance, as well as the material phenomena produced by the predominance and born of consciousness, are the conditionally arisen results of that condition.
In what sense is it "conascent," and in what sense is it "predominance"?
It is "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) in the sense of arising together; it is "predominant" (*adhipati*) in the sense of overcoming co-nascent phenomena.

Therein, "in the sense of arising together" means: when a phenomenon, while itself arising, causes the co-nascent phenomena to arise simultaneously with itself, [it is predominant] for those co-nascent phenomena in the sense of their arising together with itself.

"In the sense of overcoming" means in the sense of overwhelming. Just as a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti-rāja), by the power of his own merit, overcomes and overwhelms all the inhabitants of the island, bringing them under his control and causing all the inhabitants of the island to act according to his will;
so too these four states, having attained the position of sovereignty, [overcome their respective objects].
In their respective objects, they overcome and pervade the co-nascent phenomena, bringing them under their own control,
while those co-nascent phenomena likewise function under their control. Or, for example, in a stone pillar, the earth element overcomes the three elements co-nascent with itself—
the water element within the mass of water, the fire element within the mass of fire, and the air element within the mass of air.
Just as those that overwhelm cause their own state to be reached by the co-nascent elements, and those co-nascent elements go to that same state,
so too these four states, having attained the position of predominance, cause the co-nascent states to reach their own state through their own power,
and the co-nascent states go to that same state; thus it is in the sense of overcoming the co-nascent states.
Here they might say: "If there is such a thing as 'predominance' (adhipati) in the sense of overcoming co-nascent states, then let it be;
let it be that desire (chanda) is predominant. Rather, greed (lobha) itself should be predominant, for it occurs by being even stronger than desire and thus overwhelming the co-nascent states.
To this it is said: Among foolish worldlings (bālaputhujjana), greed is indeed stronger than desire.
It becomes more powerful; however, when desire (*chanda*) is more powerful than greed (*lobha*), it proceeds by overcoming the co-nascent states (*sahajātadhamma*).

For if greed alone were more powerful than desire, how could these beings—having cast aside the excellence of existence and the excellence of wealth that have fallen into the hands of greed—fulfill the dhamma of renunciation?

They would escape from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). However, because desire (*chanda*) alone is stronger than greed (*lobha*), these beings—having fallen into the hands of greed—exhaust their success in existence and success in wealth, and by fulfilling the state of renunciation (*nekkhammadhamma*), they escape from the suffering of the round. Therefore, desire alone is stronger than greed; it is desire...
Thus, it is predominance, not greed. This same method applies to hatred and the others as well.
In this regard, when great and very difficult tasks for men arise in the world, these four qualities lead to the successful accomplishment of those tasks.
How so? When people of inferior aspiration see great and very difficult tasks for men, their aspirations turn back.
Those who do not wish to perform it set it aside with indifference, thinking, "This is not within our domain.
However, one who is dominated by desire, upon seeing such tasks for men, becomes filled with intense longing and wishes to perform them exceedingly;
he forms the determination, "This is my domain. Driven by that desire, as long as that task is not completed, [he persists].
It is not possible to exhaust that karma in the interim. And this being so, even that very great karma will be accomplished at one time.
Furthermore, seeing such karmas, people of weak energy turn back from their effort, thinking: "This karma of mine..."
Thinking, "Much physical or mental suffering will arise for one who performs this," they turn back.
However, one who excels in energy, upon seeing such manly tasks, becomes possessed of exalted energy; he wishes to rise up and do it right now.
Even while performing that task for a long time, though experiencing much physical or mental suffering, he persists.
He does not grow weary in that work of diligence; he is unable to be without great energy in his task.
Spending day and night with such diligence, he experiences mental happiness.
And this being so, even that very great task will be accomplished in a single period of time.
Most people, being of inferior mind, upon seeing such deeds, turn their hearts away;
they do not even take them as an object of contemplation again. But one who is superior in mind, upon seeing such deeds, becomes uplifted in heart;
he is unable to dispel that thought, and his mind remains constantly bound to it. Being under the sway of that thought, for a long time...
While performing that action, one experiences much bodily suffering; this and more should be stated according to the method of the predominance of desire (*chandādhipati-naya*).
Furthermore, when people of dull wisdom see such actions, their wisdom turns back;
they do not perceive the beginning of these actions, nor do they perceive the end; they are as if entering into darkness, unable to perform those actions.
Even his mind does not incline [toward such deeds]. However, one who is preeminent in wisdom, upon seeing such actions, becomes possessed of exalted wisdom;
he sees the beginning of actions, he sees the end, he sees the fruit, and he sees the benefit. Through the successful accomplishment of action, he also perceives various means.
Thus, by performing that action even for a long time, and so forth—this is according to the method of the predominance of energy (*vīriyādhipatinaya*).
It should be said. Furthermore, it should be stated here as "by means of a great investigation of action" and "by means of such an investigation of action.
Thus, when great and very difficult human tasks are presented in the world, these four factors lead to the accomplishment of those actions.
And because of the presence of these four predominant factors, there are distinguished persons in the world.
There are those who appear as omniscient Buddhas, those who appear as omniscient Bodhisattvas,
those who appear as Pacceka-Buddhas, those who appear as Pacceka-Bodhisattvas, and those who appear as chief disciples, great disciples, and disciple-Bodhisattvas.
It is by means of such distinguished persons in the world that there exists [the teaching] for the welfare and benefit of the world of beings.
Various specialized crafts for the sake of happiness and various objects of enjoyment are seen [to exist]. The exposition of the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) is concluded. 4.
Proximity Condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
What is the proximity condition? A collection of mind and mental factors that has ceased in the immediately preceding moment is the proximity condition.

Which phenomenon is the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna) of the proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya)? The aggregate of consciousness and mental factors that arises in the very next moment is the conditionally arisen of that condition.

Within a single existence, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) is the proximity-condition for the first life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta), and the first life-continuum consciousness is the proximity-condition for the second life-continuum consciousness, and so forth; this is how it should be stated.
However, when in the *Dhammayamaka* it is said, "When the second unwholesome consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa deities is occurring," according to the method already explained...

In that being, with reference to his own newly acquired personal existence (*attabhāva*), there arises a mind accompanied by craving for becoming (*bhavanikanti-taṇhā*) that occurs as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self.

At that time, first, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) vibrates twice. Then, a mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana-citta*) arises. Following that, seven impulsion moments (*javana*) of craving for becoming arise.
[These moments] arise. Following that, there is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) phase.
Moreover, at that time, that being knows nothing of the present existence; rather, he remains recollecting an object experienced by himself in a previous existence.
However, because the physical basis (vatthu) is exceedingly weak, that object remains quite indistinct.
It exists. Taking that as its object, a mind accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata-citta) occurs predominantly.
When the embryo has grown slightly and reached more than two months, then the sense-faculties such as the eye become complete.
Even so, because of the absence of conditions such as light within the mother’s womb, visual consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) and the others do not arise.
The four [other] types of consciousness do not arise; only body-consciousness and mind-consciousness arise.
That being experiences much physical pain and mental distress during the mother’s changes of posture and so forth.
At the time of birth, however, it undergoes intense suffering. Even after being born, as long as the primary material qualities (*vatthurūpa*) remain soft and have not yet reached maturity...
They do not go; rather, being extremely feeble in form, he remains lying on his back.
He does not perceive any present object. For the most part, his consciousness follows after his previous existence.
If he has come from an existence in hell, he is mostly characterized by a deformed face. His previous objects of perception were those of hell.

Depending on [the objects], his face appears distorted moment by moment. But when he has come from the world of the devas, depending on divine objects, he is mostly possessed of a serene face; his face appears smiling moment by moment.
However, when the material bases (vatthurūpa) become sharp and reach maturity, his consciousnesses (viññāṇa) become very clear.
They proceed. At that time, having become non-deluded, he remains playing, sporting, rejoicing, and delighting.
He perceives present objects; he perceives his mother’s speech. Here, consciousness following this world proceeds frequently for him.
He forgets his previous birth.
But does every single being forget their previous birth in this very place?
No, not every being forgets in this very place. Some, being excessively oppressed by the suffering of dwelling in the womb, forget while still in the womb.
Some forget at the time of birth; some forget in this very place; and some even beyond this.
One does not forget during childhood; one forgets only when grown up. Some do not forget even throughout their entire life.
There are indeed those who recollect two or three existences; these are known as "beings who remember their past births" (*jātissara-satta*).
In that regard, from the time of birth onwards, the consciousnesses of the sixfold sense-door process (*chadvārika-vīthicitta*) proceed, having present objects as their domain.
From the moment of discernment onwards, the cognitive processes of the six doors proceed in their full complement.

In every instance, each preceding consciousness that has ceased in the immediate past serves as the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for each succeeding consciousness that arises in the immediate present.
And this so-called proximity condition, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), belongs to a single [continuum].
The continuity of a being is indeed a single stream. When a being, having attained the path of arahantship, reaches the parinibbāna of the aggregates, at that very moment that stream is severed.
In what sense is it "immediate" (anantara), and in what sense is it a "condition" (paccaya)? It is immediate in the sense of being immediately followed by another phenomenon similar to itself.
In the sense of producing, it is immediate; in the sense of assisting, it is a condition.

Therein, "of that which is similar to itself" means similar to itself by virtue of having an object (*sārammaṇa*). Regarding "by virtue of having an object": a phenomenon that does not occur without an object is called "having an object";
thus, it is "by virtue of having an object. "In the sense of producing another phenomenon" refers to the preceding [condition].
Even when the mind has ceased, the momentum of its cognitive activity does not subside; it subsides only after the subsequent consciousness has arisen.
Thus, it is by way of producing a succeeding state of phenomena.
In this context, the succession of immediate conditions (*anantara-paccaya*) should be regarded as a series of preceding mothers. The subsequent...
The succession of conditions arising from that [consciousness] should be regarded as being like a succession of daughters in the female line.
This being so, one might think that even the final consciousness of the Parinibbāna of Arahants would give rise to another state (dhamma) called a rebirth-linking consciousness.
It would not give rise to it. Why? Because at that time, due to the complete subsiding of the momentum of karma and defilements, it is exceedingly more peaceful.
"Of that consciousness": thus ends the exposition of the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*).

5. The Condition of Immediate Succession (*samanantara-paccaya*): both the classification of the conditioning state and the classification of the conditioned state are similar to those of the proximity condition.
In what sense is it "immediately subsequent" (*samanantara*)? It is immediately subsequent in the sense of being perfectly without interval (*suṭṭhu anantara*).

Just as, for example, clusters of material form on stone pillars and the like, though they are joined together, possess a delimiting form in their midst because they have shape and a common genus as material phenomena;
there is indeed an interval and a gap between two such clusters of material form. It is not so [in the case of the mental continuum].
They exist in the interval between two preceding and succeeding groups of consciousness and mental factors.

Because they lack shape and form due to their nature as immaterial phenomena, and because there is no opening in space whatsoever that could serve as a delimited medium in the middle, they are entirely devoid of an interval.
Even in the world, no "interval" between two such groups is perceived.
Then these beings perceive the mind as permanent, stable, lasting, and not subject to change; thus they have the perception of permanence regarding the mind.
In this way, it is "immediately preceding" (samanantara) in the sense of being immediately contiguous.
And "in the sense of being immediately contiguous" means, as previously stated, in the sense of producing another similar state immediately following itself.

This being so, at the time of the attainment of cessation, the preceding consciousness is the consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the subsequent consciousness is the consciousness of a noble fruit (ariyaphala-citta).
Between these two consciousnesses, one remains without consciousness for even one day and night, or two days and nights, and so on, up to seven days and nights.
Even in the plane of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta-bhūmi), the death-consciousness (cuticitta) in the preceding sensual existence [is likewise].
The preceding consciousness is called the "prior mind. In the final sensual existence, the rebirth-linking consciousness is called the "final mind.
Between these two minds, for five hundred eons in the realm of non-percipient beings, the person remains without consciousness.
In that state, the two prior minds lack the causal power to produce another phenomenon similar to themselves immediately following them.

"They exist. They do not exist. However, because they are warded off by the great powers of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and aspiration (*paṇidhi*), the preceding moments of consciousness, as they cease, cease only together with their seventy concomitants in producing the immediately succeeding distinct state.
And the subsequent moments of consciousness, as they arise, do not arise at that moment in a state of direct connection; rather, after a long interval...

Thus they arise. Yet, one cannot say that merely because of this much there is no power for preceding consciousnesses to produce a different phenomenon in their immediate succession, nor can it be said that those phenomena do not qualify as "proximate conditions" (*anantara-paccaya*).
It is just as when a king has warriors; sometimes the king, knowing the right time, says, "You must not fight now."
If one were to say, "It is not the time for battle; fight only at such-and-such a time," they would then wander about without fighting.
Even so, it cannot be said that they lack the capacity to fight, nor can it be said that those men are not warriors.

Here they might say: "In this condition, because those [mental states] lack any shape or form due to their being immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), and because there is no such thing as a 'delimitation in the middle' for anything whatsoever, it was stated that they are entirely without intervals. This being so, one might object:

"Previously, under the condition of the object (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), the arising and ceasing of consciousness moment by moment were explained through the similes of the sound of a drum and the sound of a lute."

"How then are we to understand this? [The answer is: Because in the world, it is observed that even for a mere moment, various minds that are mutually contradictory undergo a succession of preceding and succeeding states. This matter has already been explained in detail previously in the *Cittayamaka-dīpanī*.
The exposition of the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) is concluded.
6. The Conditionality of Co-nascence (Sahajātapaccaya).
Both the classification of the conditioning states and the classification of the conditioned states are explained here.
All mental states (citta) and mental concomitants (cetasika) that arise together are mutually conditions by way of co-nascence, and they are also the results of co-nascent conditionality.

The aggregates of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-nāma-khandhā) and the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), which arises simultaneously with rebirth-linking, are both mutual co-nascence conditions for one another and are phenomena arisen through co-nascence.
All the great elements (mahābhūtāni) are also mutual co-nascence conditions for one another and are phenomena arisen through co-nascence.
At the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness, all kamma-born material phenomena...

Furthermore, at the time of occurrence, all material phenomena born of consciousness produced by each respective consciousness at the moment of its arising are called "conditionally arisen" (paccayuppanna) from that co-nascent consciousness.
All derived material phenomena (upādārūpa) are called "conditionally arisen" from their co-nascent primary elements (mahābhūta).
In what sense is it "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*), and in what sense is it a "condition" (*paccaya*)? It is co-nascent in the sense of arising together;
it is a condition in the sense of being supportive. Therein, "in the sense of arising together" means:

that phenomenon which, while arising, arises and originates simultaneously with the phenomena produced by its own conditions, and produces those phenomena produced by its own conditions simultaneously with itself.
He produces it; for him, that meaning is called "simultaneous arising.
Just as the sun, when rising, rises while simultaneously producing both its own heat and its own light in the world;
and just as a lamp, when burning, burns while simultaneously producing both its own heat and its own light.
It burns. In the same way, this condition, when arising, causes its own conditionally arisen phenomena to arise simultaneously with itself.
In this context, each individual phenomenon is like the sun; the phenomena associated with it are like the sun’s heat;
and the co-nascent material phenomena are like the sun’s light. Likewise, each individual material phenomenon consisting of a primary element is like the sun.
The co-nascent great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are like the heat of the sun; the co-nascent derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) are like the light of the sun.
This same method applies to the simile of the lamp as well. The exposition of the condition of co-nascence is concluded. 7.
The Condition of Mutuality (*aññamañña-paccaya*)

Among the phenomena analyzed under the condition of co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*), whichever phenomenon is designated as the "condition" is itself both the conditioning phenomenon (*paccaya-dhamma*) and the conditioned phenomenon (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*).
All mental states (*citta*) and mental concomitants (*cetasika*) are mutually conditioning phenomena for one another and mutually conditioned phenomena for one another.
The four great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are co-nascent [with derived matter] are likewise [mutually conditioning and conditioned].
They are both mutually related conditions and mutually arisen phenomena.
The rebirth-linking mental aggregates and the rebirth-linking heart-base (hadayavatthu) materiality are both mutually related conditions and mutually arisen phenomena.
The meaning is indeed easy to understand.
Just as three staffs, when propped up against one another, serve as mutual supports for each other and depend upon one another;
and when any one of them is raised, all are raised, and when any one of them falls,
all fall— in the same way, phenomena that exist in mutual dependence are to be understood.
Here they might say: "It is logical that all mental factors (cetasika-dhammas) cannot arise without obtaining the condition of mind (citta-paccaya).
Why? Because the functions of mental factors, such as contact (phassa), are preceded by the function of cognizing;
for it is said, 'Mind is the forerunner' (manopubbangamā). But it would not be logical to say that mind cannot arise without obtaining the condition of mental factors."
It is said: mental factors (cetasika-dhammā) are the auxiliary members of consciousness; therefore, without them, consciousness itself cannot even arise.
This same principle applies to the four great elements (mahābhūta) as well. However, derived matter (upādārūpa), being merely the outflow of the great elements, does not constitute auxiliary members.
[Objection: But surely nutriment-form (āhāra-rūpa) and life-form (jīvita-rūpa) [do act as auxiliaries], because they are specific conditions?
"It is an auxiliary factor for duration. It is said: it is an auxiliary factor for duration alone, not for arising.
However, in this context, what is intended as an auxiliary factor is for arising. The exposition of the mutuality condition is finished.
8. The support condition (nissaya-paccaya).

The dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya) is threefold: co-nascent dependence (sahajāta-nissaya), base-prenascent dependence (vatthu-purejāta-nissaya), and base-object-prenascent dependence (vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-nissaya).

In this regard, what is co-nascent dependence? Every co-nascent condition is a co-nascent dependence. Therefore, the classification of conditions and the classification of conditioned states therein should be understood according to the method explained under the co-nascent condition.
Furthermore, what is base-prenascent dependence? There are six bases: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, [the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base].
The eye-base, the body-base, and the heart-base—these six bases are the support for the consciousness-elements of beings at the time of their occurrence, having arisen prior [to them].
That material form which, having arisen prior, serves as a support is "base-prenascence support" (*vatthupurejāta-nissaya*). In that regard, for the mind and mental factors...
"Foundation" (vatthu) is so called in the sense of being a basis of support.
"Pre-arisen" (purejāta) means arisen at a moment prior to the moment of arising of its own respective conditionally produced phenomenon.
In that context, because the rebirth-linking consciousness lacks a pre-arisen physical foundation (vatthurūpa), it [arises] only simultaneously with itself.

It arises depending on the heart-base matter (*hadayavatthurūpa*). However, the first *bhavaṅga* consciousness arises depending on the heart-base matter that arose simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). The second *bhavaṅga* consciousness arises depending on that which arose simultaneously with the first *bhavaṅga* consciousness.
Likewise, the third *bhavaṅga* consciousness arises depending on that which arose simultaneously with the second *bhavaṅga* consciousness, and so forth.

Up until the time of death, the support by way of presence and priority (vatthupurejātanissaya) for the two elements—the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu)—is to be understood.
Just as the sounds of a lute arise only through the force of striking the strings of the lute with the lute-neck, and not otherwise;
so too, the five types of consciousness arise only when the five objects [impinge] upon the five doors known as the five physical bases.
The "impinging" (*āpāta*) occurs solely through the force of their movement, and not otherwise.
And this impinging occurs precisely at the moment those sense-doors and objects reach their state of stability.

Due to the condition of impinging, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) vibrates twice. Due to the condition of the vibration of the life-continuum, adverting (*āvajjana*) arises. Due to the condition of adverting—

And those five consciousnesses arise. Therefore, the five bases—the eye and so forth—having arisen precisely at the moment of the arising of the past *bhavaṅga* consciousness, serve as the base-prenascence condition for the five elements of consciousness.
However, at the time near death, all six bases [serve as such] prior to the death-consciousness, in relation to the seventeenth *bhavaṅga* consciousness.
They arise only at the moment of their own arising and do not arise thereafter.

Therefore, at the time near death, the life-continuum consciousnesses (*bhavaṅga-citta*), all six-door process-consciousnesses, and the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*)—having already arisen previously—arise depending upon their respective bases (*vatthu*).
This is the base-prenascence support (*vatthupurejāta-nissaya*).
What, then, is the base-object-prenascence support? When, having taken as object one's own internal base-form (*vatthurūpa*), one grasps that form by way of craving,
conceit, and views— thinking, "This is mine, this am I, this is my self"— or else thinking, "This is impermanent, this is suffering, this is non-self."
Alternatively, through the process of comprehension (*sammasana*), the mind-door cognitive series beginning with adverting (*āvajjana*) proceeds.

At that time, each respective material phenomenon serves both as the physical basis (*nissaya-vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*) for those [consciousnesses]. Therefore, each respective heart-base materiality (*hadaya-rūpa*) constitutes the base-object-prenascence condition (*vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-paccaya*) for its corresponding arising of consciousness. This is the base-object...
The pre-arisen support (*purejāta-nissaya*). Thus, the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) is threefold.
Here, the scriptural support (*suttanta-nissaya*) should also be mentioned: these humans, or animals, or trees and so forth, are established upon the great earth;
and the great earth is [established] upon the great mass of water below, and the great mass of water is [established] below...
Having understood the entire course of worldly existence—such as the great masses of wind, and how those masses of wind rest upon the cloudless sky;

humans in their houses, monks in their monasteries, and deities in their celestial mansions—the relation of support (nissaya-paccaya) is to be understood. The exposition of the relation of support is concluded. 9.
The Relation of Strong Support (upanissaya-paccaya).

The decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is threefold: object-decisive support, proximity-decisive support, and natural decisive support. Among these, the object-decisive support is similar to the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya*); the proximity-decisive support is similar to the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*).

What is the natural decisive support? All past, future, and present states—whether internal or external, including mind, mental factors, and material phenomena—as well as Nibbāna and concepts (*paññatti*), serve as the natural decisive support for all present states of mind and mental factors, each according to its suitability.
In this regard, our past Buddha who has attained final Nibbāna, the Dhamma, the Noble Sangha of disciples, and the succession of conventional Sanghas,
are the natural decisive support condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*) for the arising of wholesome states in us, their future descendants. Likewise, in the world,
deceased parents, teachers, wise recluses and brahmins, and renowned teachers of various sects [are such conditions].
Furthermore, the ancient kings of great psychic power and great majesty serve as the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) for the arising of the wholesome,
the unwholesome, or the arising of pleasure and pain among later generations.
For it was for the sake of later people that they established various proclamations of the True Dhamma or various proclamations of what is not the True Dhamma, as well as various worldly requisites.
Or they established them in the past. And later people, regarding those things established by them—whether the practices of giving, virtue, and so forth;
the worldly customs or the customs of clan and lineage; various views and doctrines; various spheres of action, spheres of craft, or fields of knowledge;
or whatever was established such as villages, towns, cities, fields, lands, ponds, lotus pools, reservoirs, and so on; or houses, chariots, carts, and boats—[they followed them].
In the world, people prosper by engaging in inheritance regarding relationships such as those of co-residents, or regarding gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth.

Likewise, the future Buddha named Metteyya, his Dhamma, and his Saṅgha are the natural *upanissaya* conditions for the current activity of the perfections and merit of many people. So too, in this very existence, at the final time—
When one will obtain the excellence of sovereignty, status, wealth, and grain in a future time,
these serve as the natural decisive support condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*) for the arising of various volitional formations among the great masses of people established in former times.

Furthermore, the excellence of existence, the excellence of enjoyments, and the excellences of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna that one will experience in a future life, [are related] to those in the present life.
For those who are established [in virtue], it is the natural decisive support condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*) for the arising of meritorious deeds such as generosity and morality.
Just as in the world, during the winter season, people undertake the work of plowing and sowing with the thought,

"We shall obtain grain and fruit," and once the work is accomplished, they undertake various acts of energy or various acts of wisdom in the preceding period with the thought, "We shall obtain this or that wealth."

Or they undertake various tasks. In this regard, the acquisition of grain, fruit, and the acquisition of various kinds of wealth are the *pakatūpanissaya* (natural decisive support) condition for those respective undertakings of work in the future;

and conversely, those respective undertakings of work are the *pakatūpanissaya* condition for the acquisition of grain, fruit, and the acquisition of various kinds of wealth in the past. It is exactly the same for the future.
Perceiving the various fruits of kamma throughout past and present times, and aspiring toward them, great masses of people undertake various meritorious deeds.
In this context, the fruits of merit are the natural decisive support condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*) for future meritorious deeds;

meritorious deeds are the natural decisive support condition for the fruits of merit that have passed. Therefore, there is both a natural decisive support condition in the future and a natural decisive support condition in the past.
It is an exceedingly great condition.

Present Buddhas are conditions for present humans, devas, and Brahmas; present mothers and fathers are conditions for present sons, daughters, and so forth. This is called the present natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
It is indeed very well-known. Internal phenomena that serve as natural decisive supports are those that have arisen within the conscious continuums of beings such as the Buddhas.

Conditions (paccayadhammā). External natural sufficing conditions (pakatūpanissaya-dhammā) refer to those things that serve as a support for beings, such as the earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth;

these are of great benefit to various beings, including forests, woods, trees, grass, rice, barley, and the like, as well as the moon, sun, planets, stars, and so forth, and rain, water, fire, wind, cold, heat, and so forth—all of these are [conditions] for beings.
They serve as powerful conditions for the arising of the wholesome, the unwholesome, happiness, or suffering.

These people either cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) with the thought, "We shall attain final Nibbāna in this very life," or they fulfill the perfections (pāramī-dhamma) with the thought, "We shall attain final Nibbāna at a future time when a Buddha appears. In that regard, Nibbāna is for them...
It is a powerful condition for the arising of phenomena.

Both the conventional designations consisting of various worldly expressions and the designations consisting of the Dhamma of the Tipiṭaka study within the Buddha’s teaching are powerful conditions for knowing their respective meanings.
In this regard, conditioned phenomena arise when there is a condition and do not arise when it is absent; even after having arisen...
"When conditions exist, they persist; when conditions do not exist, they do not persist. Therefore, a condition must be sought for their arising or their persistence.
However, Nibbāna and concepts (*paññatti*) are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṅkhata-dhammā*);
they are by nature unborn, non-arising, eternal, and stable. Therefore, there is no such thing as a condition for their arising or their persistence."

A wholesome state is the decisive support (upanissaya) for a wholesome state. This is well-illustrated by such passages as: "Relying on faith, one gives a gift, undertakes moral discipline," and so forth.

Likewise, an unwholesome state is [the support] for an unwholesome state, as shown by such passages as: "Relying on lust, one kills a living being, takes what is not given," and so forth; and by such passages as:
"Relying on a favorable season and relying on suitable food, one experiences bodily pleasure," and so forth.
That the indeterminate (abyākata) is also clearly evident as a decisive support (upanissaya) for the indeterminate;
and that the wholesome (kusala), moreover, is a powerful decisive support even for the unwholesome (akusala). Having given a gift, one exalts oneself because of that gift and disparages another.
Likewise, having become endowed with virtue (sīla), endowed with concentration (samādhi), and endowed with wisdom (paññā).
One exalts oneself and disparages another.
Skillful [states] are also a strong decisive support (*balavūpanissaya*) for the indeterminate.

All skillful kamma of the four planes, or skillful states that accompany such kamma, are a strong decisive support at a later time for the resultant-indeterminate states of the four planes. The perfection of giving...
While fulfilling them at the time of fulfillment, they experience much bodily suffering.

The same method applies to the perfection of virtue, the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of energy, the perfection of patience, the perfection of truth, the perfection of determination, the perfection of loving-kindness, and the perfection of equanimity.
This same principle also applies to the development of the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and the development of the paths (magga).

An unwholesome state is also a strong decisive support (*balavūpanissaya*) for a wholesome one. Here, someone having committed an evil deed later becomes remorseful and, in order to abandon that evil, accomplishes wholesome states such as giving, virtue, jhāna, and the path. That evil is a strong decisive support for those wholesome states.
An unwholesome state is also a strong decisive support for an indeterminate state. Here, many people, having committed misconduct, [are reborn] in the four states of deprivation.
Having fallen [into the lower realms], they experience the suffering of the woeful states (*apāya*).

Even in this present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*), some experience much suffering due to their own or another’s misconduct (*duccarita-kamma*). Some, having acquired wealth through misconduct, experience happiness.
Many people experience much suffering rooted in lust (*rāga*), and [suffering] rooted in hatred (*dosa*).
"Rooted in views, rooted in conceit.
Even that which is indeterminate can be a strong decisive support (*upanissaya*) for what is wholesome.

For instance, through the attainment of wealth, one gives gifts, fulfills morality, fulfills wisdom, and [seeks] a dwelling suitable for development—whether it be a cave, a grotto, a tree, a forest, or a mountain.
Or, having obtained a village as a resort, or a favorable climate, or suitable food, one develops this or that meditation.
The indeterminate is also a powerful decisive support for the unwholesome. In the world, based on the possession of eyes, many unwholesome states rooted in seeing arise.
This same principle applies to the possession of ears and so forth. Likewise, [it applies to] the possession of hands and the possession of feet.
It may also be described as "perfection of weapons" (*sattha-sampadā*), "perfection of arms" (*āvudha-sampadā*), and so forth. Thus, the decisive support (*upanissaya*) is threefold.

Here, the "suttanta-decisive support" (*suttantūpanissaya*) should also be mentioned; it appears in many places in such phrases as "relying upon a good friend," "relying upon a bad friend," "relying upon a village," "relying upon a forest," and so on. Furthermore, there are five types of dhammas that constitute a decisive support.

They serve as powerful conditions for the uninterrupted occurrence of the three worlds known as the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*), the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*).
And this matter has been explained by us in detail in the *Niyāmadīpanī*.

In what sense is it an object-strong-dependence condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*)? The very object that has become predominant is an object-strong-dependence condition in the sense of being a powerful support for the states that take it as their object.

In what sense is it called "proximate decisive support" (*anantarūpanissaya*)? The preceding consciousness itself is the proximate decisive support for the arising of the succeeding consciousness, in the sense of being a powerful support.
The preceding consciousness is like a mother, and the succeeding consciousness is like a son. Just as a mother [is the support] for the arising of her son immediately after herself...
Just as a support exists for the arising of a subsequent state, so too does a preceding consciousness exist for the arising of a succeeding consciousness.

In what sense is it called "natural decisive support" (*pakatūpanissaya*)? It is called "natural decisive support" because it is a decisive support well-known in the world precisely by its very nature (*pakati*).
Furthermore, the influence of the immediate decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*) extends only to the immediately following consciousness; however, the influence of the natural decisive support—
Nevertheless, it reaches even distant objects. For instance, in this very life,
objects seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, or cognized on previous days, months, or years, will— given the appropriate conditions later on—
appear at the mind-door even after a hundred years, in such ways as, "This was seen by me before," or "This was heard by me," and so forth.
Beings recollect [their past lives]. Furthermore, beings of spontaneous birth (opapātika) recollect even their previous existence.
Likewise, among humans as well, some obtain the knowledge of remembering their own births (jātissara-saññā).

Similarly, regarding objects seen and so forth throughout many hundreds of thousands of previous lives, when one subsequently sees or hears a single object at a single moment, at that very same moment [one may recollect] many of those [objects].
It proceeds pervading the continuum of mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*). The exposition of the decisive support condition (*upanissayapaccaya*) is finished. 10.
The Pre-existence Condition (*purejātapaccaya*):

The pre-existence condition is threefold: the pre-existence condition as basis (*vatthu*), the pre-existence condition as object (*ārammaṇa*), and the pre-existence condition as both basis and object (*vatthārammaṇa*).

In this context, both the object-base-prenascence (*vatthupurejāta*) and the object-object-prenascence (*vatthārammaṇapurejāta*) were already explained previously under the heading of "support-condition" (*nissayapaccaya*).
As for what is called object-prenascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*), it refers exclusively to the eighteen produced material phenomena that are present.

Among these, the five present objects—visible form, sound, and so forth—are invariably the object-prenascence condition for the five types of consciousness belonging to the fivefold sense-consciousness process.

They exist. For just as the sounds of a lute arise only by means of striking the strings of the lute with the lute-neck, and since this being so, those sounds cannot arise without the previously arisen lute-strings and lute-neck;
even so, the five types of sense-consciousness and the five-door cognitive processes [arise] in relation to the five objects at the five bases and doors.
They arise solely due to the arrival at the range [of the senses]. And this arrival at the range occurs for those two only at the moment they have reached their respective positions.
Furthermore, it is not only at that time that those five objects arrive at the range within those five bases;
rather, they also certainly arrive at the range at the mind-door (manodvāra) during the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). It is precisely because of that arrival at the range that—
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) also vibrates twice and then is cut off; it is precisely upon the cutting off of the life-continuum that those process-consciousnesses arise.
This being so, those process-consciousnesses are unable to arise without the pre-arisen bases, doors, and objects.
Furthermore, all eighteen of those produced material phenomena, having ceased, are past.
They exist; having not yet arisen, they are also future; having arisen, they are also present.

All of them serve as objects for the consciousnesses of the mind-door process (*manoviññāṇavīthi*). Among these, only those that are present serve as their object-prenascence conditions (*ārammaṇapurejāta-paccaya*).
When one perceives a particular objective basis situated at a distance or in concealment, [it is through the power of the mind that it becomes an object].
When one takes an object by means of the mind alone, then that respective basis, if it exists at that particular time and place, is called "present.
The exposition of the pre-nascence condition is finished. 11.
The post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya).
Each subsequent present consciousness is a postnascent condition for the growth and development of the preceding present material body produced by the four causes.
This is just as the rainwater falling year after year in later years serves as a postnascent condition for the growth and development of the young trees that sprouted in previous years.
In this context, "each subsequent consciousness" refers to all consciousness from the first bhavaṅga up to the death-consciousness (cuti-citta).

"Of that which has arisen prior" refers to the entire body of matter produced by the fourfold origination included within one's own internal continuum, beginning with the body of matter born of kamma that arose simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta).

For the material body born of kamma that arises simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), the first fifteen moments of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*) are related as postnascent conditions (*pacchājātapaccaya*).
However, the rebirth-linking consciousness itself is not postnascent because it arises simultaneously with that body.
Furthermore, the sixteenth moment of the life-continuum consciousness is a condition for that body because it arises within the field where that body is to perish.
It does not exist. Therefore, it is said that there are fifteen bhavaṅga consciousnesses.

However, at the moment of the subsistence (ṭhiti) of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta), two material bodies arise: the material body born of kamma (kammaja-rūpakāya) and the material body born of the physical elements (utuja-rūpakāya).
The same occurs at the moment of its dissolution (bhaṅga). But at the moment of the arising (uppāda) of the first bhavaṅga, three material bodies arise.
There is the body of matter born of kamma, the body of matter born of the primary elements, and the body of matter born of mind.

When internal nutriment, having received the diffusion of external nutriment, generates the body of matter born of nutriment, from that point on the four bodies of matter produced by the four origins proceed like the flame of a lamp.
Having passed the moment of their arising, they persist for as long as their duration lasts.
As long as they endure, those fifteen types of consciousness indeed serve as the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) for those bodies.
Regarding "growth and increase" (*vuḍḍhi-viruḷhi*): this refers to the successive growth and increase of the continuity of matter (*rūpa-santati*) originating from the four [nutriments].
For thus, if the preceding four material bodies repeatedly obtain the postnascent condition, [they continue to develop].

This being so, even as they cease, they act as powerful conditions for the increase, growth, and expansion of the subsequent succession of materiality. The exposition of the postnascence condition is concluded. 12.
The Repetition Condition (āsevanapaccaya).

The forty-seven mundane impulsion consciousnesses—namely, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, the seventeen mundane wholesome consciousnesses, and the eighteen functional consciousnesses excluding the two types of adverting consciousness—are the condition by repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*).

Among these, when a continuous stream of impulsions occurs without interruption, each preceding impulsion consciousness is a condition by repetition for the subsequent one. [This applies] up to the final [impulsion] following the four path-consciousnesses.
The final consciousness arises by way of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*).

In what sense is it "repetition"? It is in the sense of causing [the mind] to take up a period of incubation (*parivāsa*) for the purpose of increasing proficiency and for the purpose of increasing its strength and power through successive stages.
In this context, "proficiency" is like the easy occurrence of a scriptural recitation that has been rehearsed again and again.

The "functioning" (*pavatti*) refers to the effortless occurrence of each successive consciousness within the specific distinction of place and function known as the "impulsion stage" (*javana-ṭṭhāna*) and "impulsion function" (*javana-kicca*).
"Perfuming" (*parivāsa*) is like repeatedly perfuming silk cloth with fragrance;
it is the repeated perfuming of the mental continuum by means of passion, hatred, and so forth, or by means of non-passion, non-hatred, and so forth. In the former [case]...
Even when the impulsion consciousness has ceased, its momentum does not cease; rather, it continues to proceed, pervading the subsequent stream of consciousness.
Therefore, each succeeding impulsion consciousness that arises, being sustained by that momentum, arises with even greater strength.
In this way, the preceding consciousness causes the succeeding consciousness to take up its own legacy.
The subsequent consciousness proceeds by taking up the continuity of the preceding consciousness.
Even so, that momentum of repetition naturally comes to an end after seven mental moments;
thereafter, either a resultant consciousness with that same object arises, or the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness resumes its course.

Here, the condition of "cultivation through repetition" (*sevanapaccaya*) should also be stated. It is mentioned in many places, such as: "He develops the foundation of mindfulness; he develops the right effort;
he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor; he develops the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor;
he develops right view; he develops right intention," and so forth. In that context, "he develops" (*bhāveti*) means [even] for a single day.
He develops [it]; he develops it for seven days, he develops it for one month, he develops it for seven months, he develops it for one year, or he develops it for seven years—this is the meaning.

Wholesome or unwholesome states that were practiced, developed, and cultivated in successive previous existences serve as the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*) for the arising of stronger wholesome or unwholesome states in subsequent existences.

The condition for the arising of such wholesome or unwholesome states either at another time or in another existence is called the *upanissaya-paccaya* (decisive support condition). The condition for making those very same states more powerful is called the *āsevana-paccaya* (repetition condition).

Even in the world, regarding great mental cultivation (*citta-bhāvanā*), verbal cultivation, bodily cultivation, and the cultivation of limbs and members, as well as in the spheres of action (*kamma-āyatana*), fields of craft (*sippa-āyatana*), and branches of science (*vijjā-ṭhāna*), repetition, cultivation, and frequent practice possess the quality of being a natural outflow (*nissanda-guṇa*).
They indeed appear as such.
Because such a condition of repetition exists among all momentary phenomena,
human actions that have proceeded for a long time by way of the progressive increase of human strength and human power reach their fulfillment.
They even attain the state of an omniscient Buddha. The exposition of the condition of repetition is finished. 13.
Kamma-condition:
The kamma-condition is twofold: the co-nascent kamma-condition and the asynchronous kamma-condition.

In this context, all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate volitions (cetanā) that possess the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution] constitute the co-nascent kamma-condition (sahajāta-kamma-paccaya).

All mental states and mental factors associated with volition, as well as the material phenomena born of kamma (kammaja-rūpa-dhamma) that arise simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta),
and all mind-born material phenomena (cittaja-rūpa-dhamma) during the course of existence (pavatti-kāla), are the phenomena arisen from that condition (paccayuppanna).

Past wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) is the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānā-khaṇika-kamma-paccaya*). The thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness and mental factors, as well as all material phenomena born of kamma, are the things arisen through that condition.
In what sense is it "kamma"? It is kamma in the sense of a specific kind of action (*kiriyā-visesa*). For volition is a specific kind of action because of its primacy among all actions.
Indeed, when all bodily, verbal, and mental actions are present, it is volition that constitutes each respective action.
It intends, prepares, and coordinates the associated mental states for the sake of their accomplishment; it raises them up as one. Therefore, it is the eldest among all karmas.
Thus, it is called "karma" in the sense of being a specific kind of activity (*kriyā*). Or else, it is karma because "one acts by means of it.
What does one act? One acts through bodily activity, one acts through vocal activity, and one acts through mental activity.
They perform [actions]. Therein, bodily action (*kāyikakiriyā*) refers to going, standing, sitting, and so forth;
advancing and retreating, and even, at the very least, the raising and lowering of the eyelids. Vocal action (*vācasikakiriyā*) refers to the activity of setting speech in motion.

Mental action (*mānasikakiriyā*) refers to the activities of well-considered or ill-considered thoughts, and even, at the very least, the functions of seeing and hearing performed by the five types of sensory consciousness.
All these activities are performed and undertaken by beings through this volition; therefore, that volition is called "kamma.
It arises together with that which has arisen from its own conditions, thus it is "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*). Being both co-nascent and kamma, it is "co-nascent kamma" (*sahajātakamma*).
Being a condition by way of being co-nascent kamma is "co-nascent kamma-condition" (*sahajātakamma-paccaya*). What is meant is: a condition by virtue of the state of being co-nascent kamma.
The moment of the arising of the action (*kamma*) is one thing, and the moment of the arising of its result (*vipāka*) is another;

thus, because it has separate moments of arising, it is called "belonging to different moments" (*nānākkhaṇika*). That which is both "belonging to different moments" and an "action" is "action belonging to different moments" (*nānākkhaṇikakamma*).

Being a condition while being an action belonging to different moments is the "condition of action belonging to different moments" (*nānākkhaṇikakammapaccaya*). It is a condition by way of being a condition of action belonging to different moments.
This has been stated. Volition associated with the Noble Path produces its Noble Fruit as a result (vipāka) in the very moment immediately following its own cessation;
that [volition] is likewise asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika).
And herein, a single wholesome volition of giving, together with the mind and mental factors co-nascent with itself, and with those consisting of bodily and vocal actions—

And there is the co-nascent kamma-condition for the material phenomena born of consciousness. By means of that volition, there is the asynchronous kamma-condition for the aggregates of result (vipāka) arising at a future time and for the aggregate of material phenomena born of kamma.
Thus, a single volition of good or bad conduct that has reached the state of a path of action serves as two conditions for the two types of conditionally arisen phenomena in two different times.
"By means of the powers of conditions, it becomes a condition.
And here, in the case of the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), "kamma" refers to a specific kind of action (*kiriyā*).

Even though that volition (*cetanā*) has ceased, it does not cease [along with it], but rather continues to follow that mental continuum (*cittasantāna*). When it finds the opportunity to ripen, then—
That specific kamma, having become a single individual existence (*attabhāva*) in the interval between deaths, ripens and manifests.
However, when it does not find an opportunity [to manifest], it follows that same continuum even through a hundred existences, a thousand existences, or a hundred thousand existences.
But when sublime kamma (*mahaggatakamma*) finds an opportunity, it manifests as a single Brahma-existence in the second existence, in the Brahma-world.
It ripens and manifests. However, because the karma is fully matured, it is exhausted in the very second existence and does not follow beyond that.
The exposition of the kamma-condition is finished. 14. The Ripening Condition (Vipāka-paccaya)
The thirty-six kinds of resultant co-nascent mental states and mental factors are the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*). These same states,
as well as the kamma-born material phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking, and the mind-born material phenomena produced by resultant consciousness during the course of existence,
are those arisen through the resultant condition.

In what sense is it called "result" (*vipāka*)? It is a result in the sense of having ripened (*vipaccana*). Ripening means reaching the state of being fully matured after having passed beyond the state of softness and youthfulness.
But for which phenomenon is there the state of softness and youthfulness, and for which is there the state of being fully matured?

For past karma, which is designated as the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), there is the state of softness and youthfulness; and for that very same karma, there is the state of being fully matured.

In this regard, there are four stages for a single action: the stage of volition (*cetanā*), the stage of the basis (*vatthā*), the stage of the sign (*nimittāvatthā*), and the stage of fruition (*vipākāvatthā*).

Therein, even though that volition has ceased, its specific activity does not cease; it simply continues to follow that stream of consciousness (*cittasantāna*). This is called the "stage of action. As for the "stage of the sign":
when that action gains the opportunity to ripen, at that time—specifically at the moment near death—it [manifests].
For that person, either that very same kamma manifests; at that time, the person appears as if they were giving a gift, observing virtue, or committing the taking of life.
Or else the sign of the kamma (*kamma-nimitta*) manifests—either the object such as the material for a gift, or a weapon, or some other object that served as an instrument for that kamma in the past.
Then it is as if it has come into the hands of that person.

Either the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) appears, or the object to be obtained or experienced in the rebirth—such as a celestial mansion (*dibbavimāna*) and so forth, or the mass of flames of hell—is seen at that moment.
These are called the "bases of the signs" (*nimittavatthu*).

Regarding the "state of fruition" (*vipākāvasthā*): if that person dies while not relinquishing a single object—whether it be that karma, the sign of karma (*kamma-nimitta*), or the sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*)—as it thus presents itself, then that karma ripens in that existence.
That karma manifests as a single individuality (*attabhāva*) in that existence. Among these, in the first three states:
That karma is in a state of softness and youthfulness; however, having reached its final stage of fruition, it becomes fully ripened.
Therefore it is said that "ripening" (*vipaccana*) means reaching the state of being fully ripened by transcending the state of softness and youthfulness.
Thus, the collection of mental states and mental factors that has reached this state of full ripening is called "resultant" (*vipāka*).

In this context, just as mango fruits, when they reach the state of full ripeness, become entirely smooth in appearance, even so those things subject to fruition (vipākadhammā), having become effortless and inactive, become entirely tranquil in appearance.
Precisely because of their tranquil appearance, the object of the life-continuum consciousnesses (bhavaṅgacitta) remains unmanifest; and at the time of emerging from the life-continuum—

One does not know that object. For instance, when one is sleeping at night, although the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-sota) proceeds by taking as its object the kamma or other objects grasped at the time near death in a previous existence, there arises for that person no consciousness of the cognitive process (vīthi-citta) that knows:
"This is the specific object I saw in my previous existence," with reference to that stream of the life-continuum and its object.
It is not a condition for arising. That person does not recognize that sign established in the previous existence, neither at the time of sleeping nor at the time of waking.
Thus, being helpful by way of its state as an internal form that is effortless and inactive is what is called "resultant conditionality" (*vipākapaccayatā*).
The exposition of the resultant condition is finished.
15. Nutriment Condition (Āhāra-paccaya). There are two kinds of nutriment condition: material nutriment condition and immaterial nutriment condition.
Therein, "material nutriment condition" refers to the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that is reckoned as physical food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*). And that is internal nutriment.

External nutriment is twofold. For beings who subsist on physical nutriment, all material phenomena arising from the fourfold origination are produced by conditions from those two kinds of material nutriment.
Non-material nutriment, however, is threefold: the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental volition, and the nutriment of consciousness. These three states are...
They are the nutriment-condition for co-nascent mental and physical phenomena (*nāmarūpa-dhamma*), and those co-nascent mental and physical phenomena are the dependently arisen states for them.
In what sense is it "nutriment"? It is nutriment in the sense of "carrying intensely" (*bhusaṃ haraṇa*). By "in the sense of carrying intensely," it is meant:
in the sense of causing [them] to proceed firmly, and in the sense of supporting their persistence, growth, increase, and expansion over a long period of time.
