Although food is associated with the function of producing, its primary function is that of supporting.

In this regard, material food is of two kinds; as it nourishes the material body produced by the four causes within the internal continuum, it sustains it greatly, maintains it firmly, carries it through for a long duration, and brings it to the end of each respective lifespan—thus it is called "food" (āhāra).
The nutriment of contact, extracting the desirable and undesirable flavor from objects, carries the associated states (sampayutta-dhammā) away intensely.
The nutriment of mental volition, generating enthusiasm for bodily, verbal, and mental actions, carries the associated states away intensely.
The nutriment of consciousness, performing its pioneering function in the sense of cognizing objects, [carries the associated states] away intensely.
It carries, it causes to proceed firmly, and it makes one go for a long duration; thus it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*).
Carrying the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) intensely, it likewise carries the co-nascent material phenomena (*sahajāta-rūpa-dhamma*) intensely.
Here, the method of the Suttanta should also be stated: just as birds, having discerned the cardinal and intermediate directions with their eyes, [fly] with their wings...
Just as birds leap from tree to tree and forest to forest through the air, peck at fruits with their beaks,
and sustain themselves for as long as they live; so too do these beings, having discerned objects by means of the six consciousnesses,
exert effort by means of the six volitional formations of mind for the sake of obtaining the basis of those objects, [and thus subsist] by means of the six nutriments of contact.
By making the flavor manifest within objects, they experience pleasure and pain. Or, by discerning objects through consciousnesses, they accomplish the perfection of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

By means of contacts (*phassa*), they cause the flavor to manifest within objects, and having brought about feeling (*vedanā*)—which is the experiencing of the flavor of the object—they arrive at the expansion of craving (*taṇhā*). Through volitions (*cetanā*), [they perform] those things rooted in craving...
Having produced various kamma-formations, they transmigrate from one existence to another. Thus, the great function of nutriment among things that have the nature of nutriment should be understood.
The exposition of the nutriment condition is finished. 16.
The Faculty Condition (Indriya-paccaya)

The faculty condition (indriyapaccaya) is threefold: the co-nascent faculty condition (sahajātindriyapaccaya), the pre-nascent faculty condition (purejātindriyapaccaya), and the material life-faculty condition (rūpajīvitindriyapaccaya).
Among these, fifteen dhammas consisting of faculties are called the co-nascent faculty condition:
the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the pleasure-faculty, the pain-faculty, the joy-faculty, the grief-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, and the faith-faculty... [and so forth].

The faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known.
The co-nascent states of consciousness and mental factors, as well as material phenomena, are the conditionally arisen for these.

The five material faculties—the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, and body-faculty—are the prenascent faculty-condition; the fivefold consciousness, together with its associated mental factors, are the conditionally arisen for them.

The single material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*) is a condition by way of being a material life-faculty condition. All kamma-born material phenomena, with the exception of the material life-faculty itself, are the states arisen through that condition.
In what sense is it a "faculty" (*indriya*)? It is a faculty in the sense of sovereignty (*issariya*). Wherein does its sovereignty lie?
Its sovereignty lies in the states arisen through its own respective conditions. In what specific function does its sovereignty lie? In its own...
It has sovereignty over its own function. Name-life (nāmajīvita) has sovereignty over the function of living of the associated states.

"Function of living" means the function of increasing vitality (*āyu*), that is, the function of maintaining continuity for a long duration. The mind-faculty (*manindriya*) has sovereignty over the associated states in their function of apprehending an object.
The remaining meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) has already been explained previously in the *Indriyayamakadīpanī*.

Here one might ask: "Since the two factors of the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the male faculty (*purisindriya*) are indeed faculties, why are they not included separately as faculty-conditions (*indriya-paccaya*)?

It is because of the absence of the function of a condition (*paccaya-kicca*). For the function of a condition is threefold: the function of producing (*janana-kicca*), the function of supporting (*upatthambhana-kicca*), and the function of maintaining (*anupālana-kicca*). Among these, that which is a condition for a phenomenon produced by that condition...

The function of a condition is called the "function of producing" when it is a condition for the arising [of a phenomenon], such that in its absence the conditionally arisen phenomenon does not arise;

for example, the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*). A condition which is a condition for the stability, growth, and development of the conditionally arisen phenomenon, such that in its absence the conditionally arisen phenomenon does not persist, [is called the function of maintaining].
It does not increase nor does it grow; its function as a condition is called the function of support, just like the post-nascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).

That condition which serves as a condition for the occurrence of a conditioned phenomenon (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*), without which the conditioned phenomenon would not persist for long and its continuity (*santati*) would be severed—its function as a condition is the function of maintenance (*anupālana-kicca*).

Namely: just as material form is a condition for the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). However, these two faculty-phenomena do not even accomplish a single function among those three conditional functions;
therefore, these two phenomena are not included separately under the "faculty-condition" (*indriya-paccaya*).

This being the case, should it not be said that these two phenomena are not "faculties"? It should not be said that they are not. Why? Because the function of a faculty (*indriya-kicca*) is present in them.
What, then, is the function of these faculties? Sovereignty over the gender-signs, marks, gestures, and deportment is the function of the faculty.

For instance, in the continuum of a person in whom the female-faculty-form arises at the moment of rebirth-linking, the five aggregates—arisen through the four conditions beginning with karma—evolve into the state of femininity.
That personal existence is exclusively associated with the female gender, the female characteristic, female gestures, and female appearance, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the materiality of the female faculty does not produce those five aggregates, nor does it support them, nor does it preserve them;
rather, those phenomena arise in such and such ways through their own respective conditions.
As if issuing a command, "Let them arise," it exercises its own sovereign power over them; and those phenomena arise exactly in that way and not otherwise.
This is the sovereignty of the female-faculty materiality (*itthindriya-rūpa*) over the female characteristics and so forth.

The same principle applies to the sovereignty of the male-faculty materiality (*purisindriya-rūpa*) over the male characteristics and so forth. Thus, these two phenomena perform the function of a faculty (*indriya-kicca*) with respect to the characteristics and so on.
Because of their existence, they are called "faculties" (*indriya*).

However, although the heart-base matter (*hadayavatthu-rūpa*) fulfills the function of being the physical support for two consciousness-elements, it does not fulfill the function of a faculty with respect to them.
For even in the case of a person whose mind is cultivated, there is no clarity within the heart-matter.
Even when non-faith arises, the mind-consciousness elements follow along with it. The exposition of the faculty-condition is finished. 17.
The Jhāna-condition:
The seven jhāna factors are the jhāna-condition: applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), mental joy (somanassa), mental grief (domanassa), and equanimity (upekkhā).

One-pointedness (*ekaggatā*). The mental and mental-concomitant phenomena, as well as material phenomena, that arise together with these [factors]—excluding the fivefold sense-consciousness—are its "condition-produced" (*paccayuppanna*) states.
In what sense is it called "meditation" (*jhāna*)? It is meditation in the sense of closely contemplating (*upanijjhāyana*). "In the sense of closely contemplating" means by means of the mind.
It is by way of contemplating and by way of observing after having approached the object.

For just as an archer, standing at a distance and wishing to shoot an arrow into a small target circle, does so by making the arrow straight and steady with his hands, making the circle distinct, and contemplating it with his eye;
even so, by these factors, the mind is made straight and...
Having made [the mind] steady and having made the object clear, the person who contemplates is said to "contemplate closely.
Having contemplated closely in this way, whatever bodily action, verbal action, or mental action he performs, he performs it without failing.
Therein, "bodily action" refers to such things as advancing and retreating; "verbal action" refers to that which is complete in syllables and phonemes.
The manifestation of speech is what is called verbal action. Mental action is said to be whatever discernment of an object occurs by means of the mind.
Whether it be the act of giving or the act of taking life, it cannot be performed with a weak mind that lacks the corresponding factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*).
This same principle applies to all other wholesome and unwholesome actions.
And this meaning should be illustrated by the individual intrinsic natures and characteristics of the factors of absorption, beginning with applied thought (*vitakka*).
Applied thought has the characteristic of directing the associated states toward the object; it firmly applies the mind to the object.
Sustained thought (*vicāra*) has the characteristic of continued mental engagement with the object; it firmly binds the mind to the object.

Rapture (pīti) has the characteristic of relishing the object; it makes the mind thoroughly satisfied with the object. The three kinds of feeling also have the characteristic of experiencing the flavor of the object;
they too make the mind firmly bound to the object through their function of experiencing desirable, undesirable, and neutral flavors.
One-pointedness (ekaggatā) has the characteristic of centering; it also [makes the mind] [firmly bound to the object] with respect to the object.
"Having made it immovable, he establishes it. The exposition of the condition of jhāna is finished. 18.
The Condition of the Path:
The twelve path-factors are the path-condition: right view, right intention, right speech, and right action.
Right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration.
The remaining three—wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood—are not separate mental factors (cetasika-dhamma).
They are merely names for the four unwholesome aggregates (akusala-khandha) that proceed by way of false speech and so forth. Therefore, they...

The path-condition is not taken separately. All root-cause-accompanied cittas and mental factors, as well as the material phenomena co-nascent with those root-cause-accompanied cittas, are the "arisen by way of condition" for that [path].
In what sense is it the "path"? It is the path in the sense of leading to the destinations of happy rebirths, miserable rebirths, and Nibbāna. [It consists of] right view and the rest.
For indeed, the eight factors of the right path lead to the attainment of both the direction and destination of a happy rebirth (*sugati*) and the direction and destination of Nibbāna.
The four factors of the wrong path lead to the attainment of the direction and destination of an unhappy rebirth (*duggati*).
In that context, the condition of *jhāna* makes the mind straight toward the object, makes it firm, and brings it to the state of absorption (*appanā*).
"Attained to absorption" (appanāpatta) means that the mind has entered into the object of the sign, such as the kasiṇa-sign, just like a fish cast into deep water;

this is what is called "attained to absorption. The condition of the path straightens, strengthens, and brings to the state of a full path both the volitional action on the path of the round and the action of development on the path of the turning-away, bringing about their growth and increase.
It brings about expansion; it reaches another plane of existence. This is the distinction between these two conditions.

In this context, "reaching the path of action" refers to volitional action that has reached the course of kamma—defined as the state capable of producing rebirth-linking through the fulfillment of the factors of wholesome and unwholesome kamma such as killing living beings and so forth. "Reaching another plane of existence" [refers to...]

The "development by way of sequence" refers to the work of development that, starting from the sensual plane up to the supramundane plane, reaches higher and higher stages even within a single course of action.

And this meaning should be illustrated by the individual specific characteristics of the path factors—right view and the rest—in accordance with the method explained under the condition of jhāna. The exposition of the path condition is concluded.
19. The Conditioned Relations:
Associated Condition and Dissociated Condition constitute one pair of difficulties. Presence Condition and Absence Condition constitute one pair of difficulties.
Disappearance Condition and Non-disappearance Condition constitute one pair of difficulties. These are the three pairs of difficult conditions.
There are no distinct individual conditions. Among the conditions that have arisen previously, some attain the status of a condition by being associated with their own conditionally-arisen states;
some do so by being dissociated; some by being present; some by being absent; some by having passed away; and some by not having passed away.
These three types of suffering regarding conditions have been stated for the purpose of vision.

Furthermore, in such passages as "‘It exists,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme; ‘it does not exist’ is the second extreme," the terms "exists" and "does not exist" function with reference to eternalism and annihilationism.
Therefore, [these three types of suffering] are taught for the purpose of turning away from such positions.
Furthermore, it is said that [the mind] is free from suffering.
All co-nascent states of consciousness and mental factors are both conditions for one another and the products of those conditions.

In what sense are they "associated"? They are "associated" (sampayutta) because, being endowed with these four factors of association—arising together, ceasing together, having the same basis, and having the same object—they are conjoined and have attained a state of unity.
In this context, "having attained unity" means that eye-consciousness has attained unity with the seven mental factors beginning with contact;
thus, it receives the single designation of "seeing. These eight phenomena do not receive separate designations, nor is it possible to discern them by separating them out.
This same method applies to all other types of consciousness.
The exposition of the associated condition is finished. 20.
The dissociated condition:
The dissociated condition is fourfold—conascent, base-prenascence, object-prenascence, and postnascence.

Therein, "conascent dissociation" means that, among the two—name and form—which are the conditioned and the conditionally arisen through the conascence-condition, either name is a condition for form by way of being dissociated from it, or form is a condition for name by way of being dissociated from it. Therein, "name" refers to the four aggregates as name during the course of existence;
"for form" refers to mind-produced form; and "form" refers to the heart-base at the moment of rebirth-linking.
"Of name" means of the four aggregates of rebirth-linking that constitute name. The remaining three types of dissociation conditions have already been analyzed above.
The exposition of the dissociation condition is concluded. 21.
The Presence Condition (atthipaccaya).

The presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) is sevenfold: co-nascent presence condition (*sahajāta-atthipaccaya*), base-precedent presence condition (*vatthu-purejāta-atthipaccaya*), object-precedent presence condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta-atthipaccaya*),

base-and-object-precedent presence condition (*vatthu-ārammaṇa-purejāta-atthipaccaya*), post-nascent presence condition (*pacchājāta-atthipaccaya*), material nutriment presence condition (*rūpāhāra-atthipaccaya*), and material life-faculty presence condition (*rūpa-jīvitindriya-atthipaccaya*).

In this context, the *sahajāta-paccaya* (simultaneous condition) itself is called the *sahajāta-atthi-paccaya* (simultaneous-presence condition). This same method applies to the remaining six [conditions]. The distinction between the condition and the conditioned has already been explained in various places above.

In what sense is it the "presence condition"? It is the presence condition because it acts as a condition for a phenomenon that is present by way of its own state of existence, characterized as momentary presentness. The exposition of the presence condition is finished. 22. The Absence Condition (*natthi-paccaya*)
23. Disappearance Condition (vigatapaccaya) 24.

Non-disappearance Condition (avigatapaccaya) All proximate conditions (anantarapaccaya), absence conditions (natthipaccaya), and likewise disappearance conditions (vigatapaccaya), as well as non-disappearance conditions (avigatapaccaya), are [included herein].
The presence condition (atthi-paccaya) is identical to all others [in its application]. "Presence" (atthi) and "non-disappearance" (avigata) are one and the same in meaning;
likewise for "absence" (natthi) and "disappearance" (vigata). The exposition of the absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance conditions is concluded.
The exposition of the meanings of the conditions is concluded.
The Homogeneity of Conditions (paccayasabhāga) is now explained. There are fifteen types of co-nascence (sahajāta):
four great co-nascences, four intermediate co-nascences, and seven minor co-nascences. Among these, the four called "great co-nascences" are as follows: co-nascence...
Co-nascence-dependence (sahajātanissaya), co-nascence-presence (sahajāta-atthi), and co-nascence-non-disappearance (sahajāta-avigata). The four intermediate co-nascences are called:
mutuality (aññamañña), result (vipāka), association (sampayutta), and co-nascence-dissociation (sahajāta-vippayutta). The seven minor co-nascences are called:
root (hetu), co-nascence-predominance (sahajāta-adhipati), co-nascence-kamma (sahajāta-kamma), co-nascence-nutriment (sahajāta-āhāra), co-nascence-faculty (sahajāta-indriya), jhāna, and path (magga).
There are three material nutriments: the nutriment of form, the presence of the nutriment of form, and the absence of the nutriment of form.
There are three material life-faculties: the life-faculty of form, the presence of the life-faculty of form, and the non-absence of the life-faculty of form.
Seventeen are born as pre-arisen: six are pre-arisen by way of the physical basis, six are pre-arisen by way of the object, and five are pre-arisen by way of both the physical basis and the object.
In this context, there are six types of "base-prenascence" (*vatthupurejāta*):

base-prenascence, base-prenascence-support, base-prenascence-faculty, base-prenascence-dissociation, base-prenascence-presence, and base-prenascence-non-disappearance. There are six types of "object-prenascence" (*ārammaṇapurejāta*):
object-prenascence, certain objects as predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*), and certain objects as decisive support condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*).

Object-prenascence-existence; object-prenascence-non-disappearance. In such phrases as "some object" (*kiñci ārammaṇaṃ*), the word "some" (*kiñci*) and similar terms refer to present, produced material form (*nipphanna-rūpa*).
There are five types of object-prenascence: object-prenascence, object-prenascence-support, object-prenascence-dissociation, and object-prenascence-existence.
The base-object-prenascence-nondisappearance [condition] consists of four types of postnascence: postnascent-postnascent-dissociation, postnascent-presence, and postnascent-nondisappearance.
There are seven types of proximity: proximity, immediate-proximity, proximity-support, repetition, and proximity-kamma.
There is none that has passed away. Herein, "immediately preceding kamma" refers to the volition of the Noble Path; it produces its own Noble Fruit immediately after itself.

There are five [types of] conditions separately: the remaining object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the remaining predominance of object (*ārammaṇādhipati*), the remaining object-proximity-support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), all natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), and the remaining asynchronous kamma (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma*). Thus, in detail, are the conditions of the *Paṭṭhāna*.
There are fifty-four divisions.

Among them, all those of co-nascent origin, all those of pre-nascent origin, all those of post-nascent origin, material nutriment (*rūpāhāra*), and the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*)—these are called present conditions (*paccuppanna-paccaya*).
All those of immediate (contiguous) origin and all those of asynchronous (different-time) origin...
“Kamma” refers to these past conditions. “Object” and “natural decisive support” (pakatūpanissaya) are both of the three times and also timeless by way of Nibbāna and concepts (paññatti).
These two phenomena—Nibbāna and concept—are called “without condition” and “unconditioned. Why? Because they are unarisen.
For those things which have what is called birth and what is called arising, they are indeed "with conditions," "conditioned," and "dependently arisen.

These two states (the Nibbāna-element with and without remainder), however, because they are without birth, without arising, and because they lack the condition of birth, are called "without conditions" and "unconditioned.
And among conditioned phenomena—which are themselves conditioned—not even a single phenomenon is permanent, stable, eternal, or of an unchanging nature.
There is no such thing as permanence. Rather, all those things are indeed impermanent in the sense of exhaustion. Why?

Because they themselves function in dependence on conditions, and because their conditions are themselves subject to the nature of impermanence. [Objection: But are not *nibbāna* and conceptual designation (*paññatti*) also conditions?
And are they not permanent and stable? [Reply: True. However, by means of the condition that is *nibbāna* alone, or the condition that is conceptual designation alone—
There is nothing called "arisen" [independently]; it has arisen solely through various conditions, and those conditions themselves are indeed impermanent and unstable.
And those phenomena which are impermanent constantly oppress and afflict sentient beings with three kinds of painful punishments;
therefore, those phenomena are indeed suffering in the sense of being fearful. In this context, the three kinds of painful punishments are as follows:
Namely, the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*).
Whatever things are impermanent—even within a single posture—they break up again and again;

how then could they be called a "self" for those beings and individuals who perceive them as permanent throughout their lives, or how could they be called "substantial"? And as for those things which are suffering...
Since they are thus [impermanent], how could those phenomena be the self of beings who are averse to suffering and desire happiness?
How could they be the core? Therefore, by virtue of being coreless, those phenomena are indeed non-self.
Furthermore, by means of this teaching on the twenty-four conditions, he demonstrates this point: all conditioned phenomena...
They exist solely in dependence upon conditions; they do not exist under the control of sentient beings.
And among those things that exist in dependence upon conditions, not even a single phenomenon arises from a few conditions; rather, it arises from many conditions.
Therefore, this teaching reaches the pinnacle of illustrating the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) of phenomena.
The Compendium of the Homogeneity of Conditions is finished.

That which is called the body-consciousness element consists of the two types of body-consciousness. The mind-element consists of the five-door adverting consciousness and the two types of receiving consciousness.
The remaining one hundred and eight types of consciousness are called the mind-consciousness element.
As for the fifty-two mental factors, they are fourfold when classified by way of groups: seven universal factors, six occasionals, fourteen unwholesome factors, and twenty-five beautiful factors.
Among the twenty-four conditions, fifteen conditions are common to all types of consciousness:
object, proximity, contiguity, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, kamma, nutriment, faculty, association, presence, absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance. For indeed—
There is no consciousness (citta) or mental factor (cetasika) that arises without an object (ārammaṇa).

Likewise, there is none that arises without the [other] conditions such as the immediately preceding condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth. Eight conditions are common conditions for certain classes of consciousness:

root-cause (hetu), predominance (adhipati), prenascence (purejāta), repetition (āsevana), result (vipāka), jhāna-factors, path (magga), and dissociation (vippayutta). Among these, root-cause (hetu)...

The root-cause condition (hetu-paccaya) is common only to those states of consciousness that arise with roots; the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) applies only to impulsion (javana) states accompanied by a predominance;

the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya) applies only to certain states of consciousness; the repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya) applies only to wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsion states; the result condition (vipāka-paccaya) applies only to resultant states of consciousness;
and the jhāna factors apply only to those states of consciousness consisting of the mind-element (manodhātu) and mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu).
The path [condition] exists only for the arising of consciousness accompanied by roots; the dissociation [condition] does not exist for the arising of consciousness in the formless world;
and the single postnascent [condition] occurs separately only for material phenomena.
Herein, this is the illustration: the seven mental factors common to all consciousnesses are called contact, feeling, perception, volition, [faith, mindfulness, and concentration].
One-pointedness is life, attention. Among these, consciousness is of the nature of predominance and is a condition as nutriment and a condition as faculty.
Contact is a condition as nutriment. Feeling is a condition as faculty and a condition as jhāna. Volition is a condition as kamma and a condition as nutriment.
One-pointedness is a condition as faculty, a condition as jhāna, and a condition as path.
Life is a faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*). The remaining two factors are not specific conditions (*visesa-paccaya*).
In eye-consciousness, seven universal mental concomitants (*cetasika*) are found; together with consciousness, there are eight mental states (*nāma-dhamma*).
All those states act as mutual conditions for one another by way of seven conditions (*paccaya*), [and] by way of four...
And with the three middle co-nascents, excluding those dissociated from the great co-nascents.
Among those same eight states, consciousness is a condition for the remaining seven states by way of nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) and faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*).
Contact is a condition by way of nutriment-condition; feeling is a condition merely by way of faculty-condition; volition is a condition by way of kamma-condition (*kamma-paccaya*).
And by way of nutriment-condition; and by way of the condition of faculty alone, one-pointedness is a condition for the remaining seven states by way of faculty-condition.

Furthermore, the eye-base materiality is a condition for those eight states by way of the six types of base-prenascence; and as for the present visible objects that have come into range within that eye-base:

For these [consciousnesses], the four [mental aggregates] are related by way of the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*); the five-door adverting consciousness that has just ceased is related by way of the five immediate conditions (*anantara*);

and wholesome or unwholesome karma performed in the past is related to those wholesome or unwholesome resultant states by way of the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*), as are the ignorance, craving, and clinging belonging to the previous existence which acted as the companions to that karma.

Furthermore, in this existence, the dwelling, the person, the season, the food, and so forth, serve as conditions for those eight states by way of the natural decisive-support condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*).
In this consciousness, six conditions—root, predominance, postnascent, repetition, jhāna, and path—are not obtained;
eighteen conditions are obtained. And just as it is in this consciousness, [so it is elsewhere].
Likewise, in the case of ear-consciousness and the others, six conditions are not obtained; eighteen conditions are obtained.
The method for the combination of conditions in the fivefold sense-consciousnesses is concluded.
Now follows the method for the combination of conditions in rootless (ahetuka) consciousness-arising.

There are six miscellaneous mental factors (cetasika), namely: initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), resolve (adhimokkha), energy (vīriya), rapture (pīti), and desire (chanda).
Among these, initial application is both a condition for jhāna and a condition for the path. Sustained application is a condition for jhāna.
Energy is of the nature of dominance and is a condition for the faculties, as well as a condition for the path. Rapture is a condition for jhāna. Desire is of the nature of dominance. Resolve—
However, it is not a specific condition (*visesa-paccaya*).

In the five types of consciousness—namely, the five-door adverting consciousness, the two types of receiving consciousness, and the two types of equanimous investigating consciousness—ten mental factors (*cetasika*) are obtained: the seven universal factors and, among the occasionals (*pakiṇṇaka*), applied thought (*vitakka*).
And sustained application (*vicāra*) and resolution (*adhimokkha*). Together with consciousness (*viññāṇa*), there are eleven mental states (*nāmadhamma*) in each case.

In these types of consciousness, the function of the jhāna factors is obtained. Feeling (*vedanā*), one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), initial application (*vitakka*), and sustained application (*vicāra*) fulfill the condition for jhāna.

However, the five-door adverting consciousness (*pañcadvārāvajjana-citta*) is a functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*); it lacks the condition of karmic result (*vipākapaccaya*). And as for asynchronous karma (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma*)...
It stands in the position of decisive support (*upanissaya*). Together with the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*), six conditions are not obtained.
Together with the jhāna condition, eighteen conditions are obtained. In the remaining four resultant consciousnesses, five conditions are not obtained.
Together with both the resultant condition and the jhāna condition, nineteen conditions are obtained.
In the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassasantīraṇa*), eleven mental factors are associated with joy;
and in the mind-door adverting consciousness, there are eleven associated with energy. Thus, together with consciousness, there are twelve mental phenomena (*nāmadhamma*).
However, in the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*), twelve mental factors are associated with both joy and energy. Together with consciousness—

There are thirteen mental states (nāmadhamma). Among them, in the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-santīraṇa*), only the factor of rapture (*pīti*) is present in excess among the jhāna factors;
as in the two preceding investigations accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), the five conditions are not obtained. Nineteen conditions are obtained.
And in the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana-citta*), only the factor of energy (*vīriya*) is present in excess, and that performs the function of a faculty (*indriya*).

It does not accomplish the functions of jhāna; it does not accomplish the functions of predominance or the path. Because it is a functional consciousness (*kriyā-citta*), there is no resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*).
As in the case of the five-door adverting consciousness mentioned previously, six conditions are not obtained along with the resultant condition.
Eighteen conditions are obtained along with the jhāna condition. This is also the case for the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda-citta*).

Because they are functional consciousnesses (*kiriyacitta*), there is no resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*); however, because they are impulsion consciousnesses (*javanacitta*), there is repetition (*āsevana*).
Thus, five conditions are not obtained along with the resultant condition, while nineteen conditions are obtained along with the repetition condition.
The method for the combination of conditions in rootless consciousness-arising is concluded.
The Method of Conditionality in Unwholesome States of Consciousness:

There are twelve unwholesome states of consciousness—two rooted in delusion (*moha*), eight rooted in greed (*lobha*), and two rooted in hatred (*dosa*). There are fourteen unwholesome mental factors (*cetasika*):
delusion, lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—this is called the "tetrad of delusion."
Greed, wrong view, and conceit—this is called the triad of greed (*lobhatikka*). Hatred, envy, avarice, and remorse—this is called the tetrad of hatred (*dosacatukka*).
Sloth, torpor, and doubt—this is called a separate triad.

Among these, the three root-phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion are the cause-condition (*hetupaccaya*); wrong view is the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*); and the remaining ten phenomena are not specific conditions (*visesapaccaya*).
In that context, there are two types of consciousness rooted in delusion (*moha*): consciousness associated with doubt (*vicikicchā*) and consciousness associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*).
In the consciousness associated with doubt, fifteen mental factors arise: the seven universal factors;
the three occasionals—applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and energy (*vīriya*); the four unwholesome mental factors rooted in delusion; and doubt itself.

Thus, together with consciousness, there are sixteen mental states (nāmadhamma). In this consciousness, both the condition of cause (hetu-paccaya) and the condition of the path (magga-paccaya) are found.
Therein, delusion (moha) is the causal condition, while applied thought (vitakka) and energy (viriya) are the path conditions.

However, because of the corruption caused by doubt (vicikicchā), one-pointedness (ekaggatā) does not fulfill the function of a faculty (indriya-kicca) nor the function of the path (magga-kicca) in this consciousness; it performs only the function of a jhāna factor (jhāna-kicca).

It accomplishes [its function]. Three conditions are obtained: the dominant (adhipati), the postnascent (pacchājāta), and the resultant (vipāka); the remaining twenty-one conditions are also obtained.

In the consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sampayutta-citta) as well, there are fifteen mental factors excluding doubt (vicikicchā) along with resolve (adhimokkha), making sixteen mental states in total. In this consciousness, one-pointedness (ekaggatā) performs the functions of both a faculty (indriya) and a jhāna factor.
It accomplishes the function of the path; three conditions are not obtained, while twenty-one conditions are obtained.

In the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed (*lobha*), however, twenty-two mental factors (*cetasika*) arise: the seven universal factors, the six occasional factors, the four factors of delusion (*moha*), the three factors of greed, and sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*). Among these—

Greed and delusion—these two roots are the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*). Desire, consciousness, and energy—these three, being of the nature of predominance (*adhipati-jātaka*), sometimes fulfill the function of predominance;
here, objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is also obtained. Volition is the kamma-condition (*kamma-paccaya*).
The three nutriments are the nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*). Consciousness, feeling, one-pointedness, vitality, and energy—these five [are the faculties].

The mental states that are faculties are the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*). The five factors of absorption—initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), feeling (*vedanā*), and one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*)—are the absorption condition (*jhāna-paccaya*).
The four path factors—initial application, one-pointedness, view (*diṭṭhi*), and energy (*vīriya*)—are the path condition (*magga-paccaya*).
Two conditions, namely postnascence (*pacchājāta*) and result (*vipāka*), are not obtained. The remainder...
Twenty-two conditions are obtained.

In the two types of consciousness rooted in hatred, having abandoned both joy (*pīti*) and the triad of greed (*lobha*), there are exactly twenty-two mental factors along with the fourfold group of hatred (*dosa*).
Hatred and delusion (*moha*) are the two roots; three are of the nature of predominance (*adhipati*); three are nutriments (*āhāra*); and five...
The faculties, the four jhāna factors, and three path factors. Here too, two conditions are not obtained;
twenty-two conditions are obtained.
The method for the combination of conditions in unwholesome consciousness-arising is finished.

The twenty-five beautiful mental factors (*kalyāṇa-cetasika*) are as follows: the three roots of goodness—non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*);

faith (*saddhā*), mindfulness (*sati*), moral shame (*hirī*), moral dread (*ottappa*), equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*), tranquility of body (*kāya-passaddhi*), and tranquility of mind (*citta-...*) [tranquility of mind].
Tranquillity and lightness of body, lightness of mind; malleability of body and malleability of mind;
wieldiness of body and wieldiness of mind; proficiency of body and proficiency of mind; rectitude of body and rectitude of mind;
right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three abstinences; and compassion and appreciative joy—these two immeasurables.

In that context, the three roots of goodness (kalyāṇamūla) are the root-condition (hetu-paccaya). Non-delusion (amoha), however, is called the predominance of investigation (vīmaṃsādhipati) under the predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya);

it is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) under the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya); and it is called right view (sammādiṭṭhi) under the path-condition (magga-paccaya). Faith is called the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) under the faculty-condition;
mindfulness is called the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) under the faculty-condition, and right mindfulness (sammāsati) under the path-condition.
Namely: the three abstinences (virati) are path-conditions (magga-paccaya); the remaining seventeen factors are not specific conditions (visesa-paccaya).
In the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses (kāma-kusala-citta), thirty-eight mental concomitants (cetasika) are included:

seven universal, six occasionals (pakiṇṇaka), and twenty-five beautiful (kalyāṇa). Among these, joy (pīti) occurs only in the four types of consciousness accompanied by gladness (somanassika), and non-delusion (amoha) [occurs in all].
The three abstinences occur only in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge;

the two illimitables occur only in the modes of compassion and sympathetic joy toward sentient beings. In these eight types of consciousness as well, two or three roots serve as the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*);
and among the four types of predominance, each one—namely desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation—is present.
Sometimes there is the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*). Volition is the kamma condition (*kammapaccaya*). The three nutriments are the nutriment condition (*āhārapaccaya*).
The eight faculties—consciousness, feeling, one-pointedness, life, faith, mindfulness, energy, and wisdom—are the faculty condition (*indriyapaccaya*).
The five jhāna factors—initial application, sustained application, rapture, feeling, and one-pointedness—are the jhāna condition (*jhānapaccaya*).
The eight path factors—wisdom, applied thought, the three abstinences, mindfulness, energy, and one-pointedness—are the path condition.
Among these eight types of consciousness, two conditions—the postnascent and the resultant—cannot be found;
the remaining twenty-two conditions are found.

In the eight functional consciousnesses that beautify sense-sphere experience (*kāmāsobhanakiriyacitta*), the three abstinences (*virati*) are not found; as with the wholesome consciousnesses, two conditions are not found, while twenty-two conditions are found.

In the eight resultant consciousnesses that beautify sense-sphere experience (*kāmāsobhanavipāka*), the three abstinences and the two illimitables (*appamaññā*) are not found. Furthermore, three conditions—the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta*), and the repetition condition (*āsevana*)—are not found; twenty-one conditions are found.

Even in the supramundane consciousnesses of the form and formless realms, there are no conditions exceeding the twenty-two. Therefore, the combination of these conditions should be understood as being the same as in the four wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*).
This being so, why are those [supramundane] consciousnesses greater and more sublime than the sense-sphere consciousness?
Because of the greatness of their repetition (*āsevana*). For those consciousnesses are accomplished through specific tasks of meditative development (*bhāvanā*); therefore, in them—

The condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) is great. Because of the greatness of repetition, the faculty-condition (*indriyapaccaya*), the jhāna-condition (*jhānapaccaya*), the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*), and other such conditions for them also become great.
Due to the progressive greatness of these conditions, those states of consciousness become progressively greater and more refined than sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmacitta*).
The method of the combination of conditions among the arising of consciousness is concluded.
The method of the combination of conditions among material groups is now stated.
There are twenty-eight kinds of material phenomena, namely, the four great elements...
Earth, water, fire, and air. The five sensitive forms are the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
The five objective forms are visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and the tangible. Therein, the tangible is threefold: earth-tangible, fire-tangible, and air-tangible.
The two modes of being are the female mode of being and the male mode of being. One [non-manifesting form].
The material quality of vitality, one heart-base material quality, one nutriment material quality, one space-element material quality, two intimation material qualities—
body intimation and speech intimation— three mutable material qualities— lightness, malleability, and wieldiness— and four characteristic material qualities—
growth, continuity, decay, and impermanence.
In that regard, six material phenomena are conditions for material phenomena: the four great elements, the life-faculty materiality, and nutriment materiality.
Among these, the four great elements are conditions for one another by way of five conditions:
by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, presence, and non-disappearance. For those that are co-nascent...
Derived material phenomena serve as conditions for one another through four conditions, excluding mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*).

Vitality-form (*jīvita-rūpa*) is a condition, by way of faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*), for the co-nascent kamma-born material phenomena. Nutritive essence-form (*āhāra-rūpa*) is a condition, by way of nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*), for all internal material phenomena, both co-nascent and non-co-nascent.

In that very context, thirteen material phenomena serve as specific conditions for mental phenomena: the five sensitive material phenomena, the seven objective material phenomena, and the heart-base material phenomenon.

Among these, the five sensitive material phenomena act toward the five elements of consciousness by way of the prenascent base (vatthu-purejāta), the prenascent faculty of the base (vatthu-purejāta-indriya), and the prenascent dissociation from the base (vatthu-purejāta-vippayutta), just as mothers do for their children.

And they are conditions. The seven objective forms (*gocararūpa*) are conditions by way of object-prenascence for the five consciousness-elements and the three mind-elements, like fathers for their sons.

The heart-base form is a condition at the moment of rebirth-linking for the two elements—the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—according to the case, like a tree for the deities dwelling in the tree.

At the time of its occurrence, it acts as a condition by way of co-nascence, support, and, for the material phenomena, by way of pre-existence of the basis (*vatthupurejāta*) and dissociation from the pre-existent basis (*vatthupurejātavippayutta*).

There are twenty-three material groups (*rūpakalāpa*). Among these, a group of material phenomena bound together by a single birth-characteristic (*jātirūpa*)—like a bundle of hair tied with a single string or a bundle of grass—is called a "composite material group" (*paripiṇḍirūpakalāpa*).

Within that, the eight factors consisting of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence (*ojā*) constitute one "universal root group" (*sabbamūlakalāpa*), also known as the "universal root octad" (*sabbamūlaṭṭhaka*).

There are nine material groups born of kamma: the life-nonad, the base-decad, the body-decad, the femininity-decad, the masculinity-decad, the eye-decad, the ear-decad, the nose-decad, and the tongue-decad.
Among these, the "life-nonad" consists of the eight fundamental [material qualities] together with the life-material quality.
This alone constitutes the fundamental nonad among the kamma-born groups. It is precisely this fundamental nonad that...
In due order, together with the eight types of material phenomena beginning with the heart-base (hadayavatthu), there are eight decads beginning with the base-decad (vatthudasaka).
Among these, four groups—namely, the life-nonad (jīvitanavaka), the body-decad (kāyadasaka), and the two sex-decads (bhāvadasaka)—occur throughout the entire body.
Therein, the "life-nonad" refers to both the digestive fire (pācakaggi) and the bodily heat (kāyaggi). The digestive fire...
The "digestive heat" (*pācaka-tejo*) is a constituent part; it functions within the stomach and fully digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.

The "bodily fire" (*kāyaggi*) is a constituent part consisting of the heat-element that pervades the entire body; it functions throughout the whole body and keeps the bile, phlegm, and blood from becoming putrid, keeping them clear.
When these two function irregularly, sentient beings become subject to many ailments.

When there is equilibrium, there is freedom from illness. Both of these [the temperature and nutritive elements] bring about the life-nonad, which provides for the lifespan of beings and provides for their beauty.
The body-decad provides for pleasant and painful contacts throughout the entire body.
The female-novads provide for all female characteristics in women; the male-novads provide for all male characteristics in men.
The remaining sets of ten, beginning with the "tissue-decad" (*vatthudasaka*), are called the "location-decads" (*padesadasaka*).
Among them, the tissue-decad, operating within the interior of the heart-enclosure (*hadayakosa*), brings about for sentient beings various kinds of well-thought and ill-thought actions.

The four decads beginning with the eye-decad—operating respectively in the eyeball, the ear-cavity, the nostril-cavity, and the surface of the tongue—perform the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting.
It brings about the modes of intimation.
There are four primary groups (mūlakalāpa): the eightfold group born of mind, the all-base octad (sabbamūlaṭṭhaka), the sound nonad (saddanavaka), and the body-intimation nonad (kāyaviññattinavaka);
and these same [groups], together with the three types of derived matter known as lightness, malleability, and wieldiness.
Together with the four groups accompanied by their modifications.
Therein, at the time when the bodily elements function unequally, for one who is ill, only the primary groups (mūlakalāpa) proceed.
For then his bodily forms become heavy, rigid, or unwieldy, according to his inclination.
It is painful even to engage in the postures, to move the limbs and members of the body, or to utter speech.
However, when the bodily elements are functioning in equilibrium, because there is an absence of bodily defects such as heaviness and rigidity in one who is not ill, they proceed with transformation.
And among those, in the movement of the body-limbs by way of the mental factor (cittanga), there are two groups of bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti).
They proceed as follows: at the time when the sound of speech issues from the mouth by means of consciousness alone, two groups of vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti-kalāpa) proceed;

at the time when sounds other than speech—such as laughter, weeping, and so forth, which are devoid of syllables and phonemes—issue from the mouth by means of consciousness alone, two groups of sound (sadda-kalāpa) proceed; and during all other times, two initial groups proceed.

There are four groups of temperature-born material phenomena (*utujarūpa-kalāpa*): two root-groups, namely the "all-root octad" (*sabbamūlaṭṭhaka*) and the "sound nonad" (*saddanavaka*), and two derivative groups (*savikāra-kalāpa*).
In this regard, this body maintains itself by following the stream of postures (*iriyāpatha-sota*) for as long as life lasts;
therefore, depending on the diversity of postures, the even and uneven occurrences of the elements (*dhātu*) within this body are discerned from moment to moment.

Likewise, it occurs due to differences in season, differences in nutriment, differences in the touch of wind and heat, differences in the maintenance of the limbs of the body, and differences in self-exertion versus external exertion.

Among these, during times of irregular occurrence, only two root-groups proceed; during times of regular occurrence, two groups accompanied by modifications proceed. And within those, there are two sound-groups.
They proceed from sounds born of mind to successive sounds, and to other various kinds of sounds in the world.

There are two material groups born of nutriment (*āhāraja-rūpa-kalāpa*): namely, the "all-base octad" (*sabbamūla-aṭṭhaka*) together with its modifications. These two groups are to be understood by way of the even and uneven material qualities produced by suitable or unsuitable nutriment.
The space element (*ākāsadhātu*) and the characteristic material phenomena (*lakkhaṇa-rūpa*)—these five types of matter are excluded from the groups. Among these, the space element...
Because it is merely a delimitation within a group (*kalāpa*), it is "freed from the group" (*kalāpamutta*).

The characteristic-forms (*lakkhaṇarūpa*) are "freed from the group" because they are merely characteristics for the purpose of knowing the conditioned state of the groups of formed matter (*saṅkhatarūpa*).
These twenty-three groups are found within the internal continuum; however, in the external continuum, there are two groups produced by the primary elements (*utujamūlakalāpa*).
Thus they are obtained. In that regard, there are two continuums of matter: the internal continuum and the external continuum.
Therein, the "internal continuum" refers to the continuum of sentient beings. The "external continuum" refers to the earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, trees, grasses, and so forth.
Within the internal continuum, twenty-eight types of matter and twenty-three material groups (rūpakalāpa) are found.
Therein, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the mental phenomena (nāmadhamma) of rebirth-linking act as conditions in six ways for the material groups born of kamma:
by way of the four great co-nascent [conditions] and by way of resultant and dissociation.

For the materiality of the heart-base, however, they act as conditions in seven ways, including mutual conditionality. Among those same mental phenomena, the causal factors act as conditions by way of being causes.

Volition acts as a condition in six ways according to its respective nature: as the state of kamma, nutriment-factors as the state of nutriment, faculty-factors as the state of faculties, jhāna-factors as the state of jhāna, and path-factors as the state of the path.
However, past wholesome and unwholesome kamma-acts act as a condition in only one way, by way of the kamma-condition; likewise for the first life-continuum consciousness and so forth.

Mental phenomena (*nāmadhamma*) that arise subsequently serve as a single type of condition for the previously arisen groups of matter born of karma (*kammajarūpa-kalāpa*) by way of the "post-nascence" condition (*pacchājāta*).
Here, by the term "post-nascence," the four types of conditions belonging to the post-nascent class are included.
Furthermore, past karmas also serve as a single type of condition. Thus, mental phenomena [serve as conditions] for the groups of matter born of karma.
They act as conditions through fourteen conditions as appropriate. Here, ten conditions are not obtained:
object, predominance, proximity, contiguity, decisive support, prenascence, repetition, association, absence, and disappearance.
At the time of their occurrence, mental phenomena that produce matter act as fivefold conditions for the groups of mind-born matter that arise simultaneously with themselves—
by way of the four great primaries and by way of dissociation. Within those very same mental phenomena, causal factors act through their nature as causes,
predominant factors through their nature as predominants, volition through its nature as kamma, and resultant phenomena through their nature as results.

Phenomena that are nutriment act as conditions in eight ways according to their respective roles: as nutriment-phenomena by way of being nutriment, as faculty-phenomena by way of being faculties, as jhāna-phenomena by way of being jhāna-factors, and as path-phenomena by way of being the Path.
All postnascent mental phenomena (nāmadhamma) act as conditions in one way—by way of postnascence—for all prenascent groups of matter born of mind. Thus do mental phenomena [act].
The groups of material phenomena born of mind act as conditions for one another through fourteen conditions, as appropriate.

Here too, ten conditions are not obtained: the object, the proximity, the contiguity, the mutuality, the decisive support, the prenascence, the repetition, the association, the absence, and the disappearance.

From the moment of the subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness onwards, during the course of its occurrence, all mental states (nāmadhamma) act as conditions in a single way—by way of post-nascence—for all groups of temperature-born material phenomena and all groups of nutriment-born material phenomena.
Here too, by the term "post-nascence," the four types of post-nascence conditions are included; the remaining twenty conditions are not applicable.
In all twenty-three groups of material phenomena (*rūpakalāpa*), the four great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) act as conditions for one another in five ways:

by way of the four great primaries arising together and by way of mutual conditionality. They act as conditions in four ways for the co-nascent derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) through the four great primaries arising together.
Nutritive materiality (*āhārarūpa*) acts as a condition for all co-nascent and non-co-nascent [derived material phenomena].
Nutriment is a condition for internal material groups by way of the nutriment-condition.

Within the nine material groups born of kamma, the life-faculty materiality is a condition for its co-nascent materialities by way of the faculty-condition. Thus, internal material phenomena are conditions for internal material phenomena in seven ways.
External material phenomena, however, [are conditions] for external primary-element material groups...
"Conditions are fivefold. Thus ends the method for the combination of conditions within material groups (*rūpakalāpa*).
Here, the meaning of the term *paṭṭhāna* must be stated: it is a "foundation" (*ṭhāna*) that is "foremost" (*padhāna*), hence *paṭṭhāna*. In this context, "foremost" means...
"Foremost" (*pamukha*) means "condition" (*ṭhāna*); thus, it is said to be the "foremost condition," the "principal condition," or the "exclusive condition.

And that exclusive condition is to be described in relation to what has arisen from an exclusive condition. For there are two kinds of things arisen through conditions: those arisen from a principal condition and those arisen from a secondary outflow (*nissanda*). Of these, that which is arisen from a principal condition—

There is that which arises from a root-condition (*mūlapaccayuppanna*), that which arises from a natural outflow-condition (*nissandapaccayuppanna*), and that which arises from a successive-condition (*paramparapaccayuppanna*). Among these, only that which arises from a root-condition is called "unilaterally arisen" (*ekantapaccayuppanna*);

for when its own condition exists, it necessarily arises and does not fail to arise. However, that which arises from a successive-condition is called "non-unilaterally arisen" (*anekantapaccayuppanna*).
For that [resultant phenomenon] arises or does not arise even when that condition is present.
In this context, a condition from which a result invariably arises is called an "invariable condition" (*ekantapaccaya*); it is precisely this that is taught in this *Mahāpakaraṇa*.
For this very reason, this group of twenty-four conditions and this *Mahāpakaraṇa* are called the *Paṭṭhāna*.
In this regard, greed arises in a certain man for the sake of wealth and grain.
Driven by that greed, he exerts himself, goes to the forest, and in a certain place cultivates fields, builds dwellings, and constructs gardens.
When these succeed, that man acquires much wealth and grain, which he enjoys for himself.
He supports his children and wife, performs meritorious deeds, and will experience the fruits of that merit in the future.
In this context, the mind-and-body (nāmarūpa) that arise together with greed are said to be "arisen from a primary condition" (*mukhyapaccayuppanna*).
Thereafter, as long as he experiences the fruits of merit in future existences, the states that arise during that time are the "successive fruits" (*paramparaphala*) of that greed.

These are called "arisen by way of outflow-condition" (*nissanda-paccaya*). Among those two types of conditionally arisen phenomena, only that which is "arisen by way of the primary condition" is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
However, that which is "arisen by way of outflow-condition" must be explained according to the method of the Suttas.
In this context, the "method of the Suttas" refers to the principle of conditionality expressed as: "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."

Furthermore, it should be stated that the three states—greed, hatred, and delusion—are called "causes" (hetu) in the sense of being the root of misfortune for the entire world of beings, the world of formations, and the world of space;
whereas the three states—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are causes in the sense of being the root of prosperity.
This same method applies to all the conditions (paccaya) in the *Paṭṭhāna*, as appropriate.

It should be understood thus: when this is the case, it should be known that all worldly processes in the world consist, together with the primary conditionally arisen phenomena, exclusively of the outflow-conditionally arisen phenomena among these twenty-four conditions.

At this point, the exposition of the *Paṭṭhāna*—which is defined by the three sections consisting of the "Exposition of the Meaning of the Conditions," the "Classification of the Conditions by Similarity," and the "Method of Combining the Conditions"—is completed.
This *Paccayuddesadīpanī* was composed by the Great Elder (*Mahāthera*) dwelling at the Leḍītīra Forest Monastery in the city of Maungdaun in the kingdom of Burma.
